p.seg: Lǎozi said:
"There is something formlessly fashioned,
that existed before Heaven and Earth.
Without sound, without substance,
it stands alone and unchanging.
It is serene and empty,
lacking nothing in its solitude.
I know not its name,
so I style it 'the Dào'.
Now this Dào,
is exalted beyond limit,
profound beyond measure.
It enfolds Heaven and Earth,
receiving the formless.
Its source flows ceaselessly,
yet it is never full.
Turbid, when stilled, gradually clears.
Applied, it is inexhaustible,
knowing neither day nor night.
Rolled up, it does not fill a hand;
contracted, it can yet expand;
obscure, it can yet shine;
soft, it can yet be firm;
it embraces yīn and emits yáng,
illuminating the three lights;
mountains rise high by it,
abysses plunge deep by it,
beasts run by it,
birds fly by it,
fish swim by it,
phoenixes soar by it,
stars and calendars move by it;
through loss it gains existence,
through humility it gains honor,
through retreat it gains precedence.
The ancient Three Sovereigns,
grasping the thread of the Dào,
stood at the center,
their spirits roaming with transformation,
to pacify the four directions.
Thus they could
make Heaven revolve and Earth stand firm,
turning like a wheel without cease,
flowing like water without end,
sharing beginning and end with all things.
Winds rise and clouds gather,
thunder rumbles and rain falls,
all responding endlessly,
once carved and polished,
returning again to simplicity.
Acting through non-action,
they harmonized with life and death;
speaking through non-speech,
they penetrated virtue and the Dào;
serene and joyful without pride,
they attained harmony;
embracing all differences,
they facilitated life.
Harmonizing yīn and yáng,
regulating the four seasons,
balancing the five phases,
moistening plants and trees,
soaking metal and stone,
beasts grew large,
fur became glossy,
birds' eggs did not spoil,
animals' wombs did not miscarry,
fathers had no worry of losing sons,
elder brothers no grief for younger brothers,
children were not orphaned,
women not widowed,
rainbows did not appear,
thieves and robbers did not arise—
all this was the effect of embracing virtue.
The constant great Dào
produces things but does not possess them,
completes transformations but does not control them.
The myriad things
depend on it to live,
yet none know its virtue;
they depend on it to die,
yet none can resent it.
Storing and accumulating
does not make it richer;
distributing and receiving
does not make it poorer.
Elusive and indistinct,
it cannot be given form;
indistinct and elusive,
its use is never exhausted;
profound and obscure,
it responds to change without form;
smooth and penetrating,
it never moves in vain;
it rolls and unrolls with firmness and softness,
it rises and falls with yīn and yáng.
Lǎozi said:
The great man is serene without thought,
tranquil without worry.
Taking Heaven as his canopy,
Earth as his chariot,
the four seasons as his steeds,
and yīn and yáng as his drivers,
he travels where there is no road,
roams without tiring,
emerges without a gate.
Taking Heaven as his canopy means nothing is left uncovered;
taking Earth as his chariot means nothing is left unborne;
taking the four seasons as his steeds means nothing is left uncommanded;
taking yīn and yáng as his drivers
means nothing is left unprepared.
Thus he moves swiftly yet steadily,
travels far yet without fatigue,
his limbs never toil,
his senses never impair,
and he illuminates all under Heaven—
this is grasping the essence of the Dào,
observing the realm of the boundless.
Therefore, the affairs of the world cannot be forced;
follow their natural course and guide them.
The transformations of the myriad things cannot be fully fathomed;
grasp their essential direction and return to it.
Thus the sage cultivates the root within,
and does not adorn the branches without.
He sharpens his spirit,
lays aside his cunning,
indifferently practices non-action, yet nothing is left undone;
practices non-governance, yet nothing is left ungoverned.
What is called non-action
is not acting before things occur;
non-governance
is not altering what is natural;
leaving nothing ungoverned
means following what is mutually so among things.
Lǎozi said:
One who holds the Dào to guide the people
follows events as they come,
responds to things as they move.
No transformation of the myriad things goes unresponded to,
no change over a century goes unpaired.
Thus the Dào
is虚无 (xūwú, emptiness),
平易 (píngyì, even and simple),
清静 (qīngjìng, clear and tranquil),
柔弱 (róuruò, soft and weak),
纯粹素朴 (chúncuì sùpǔ, pure, plain, and unadorned).
These five
are the images of the Dào.
Emptiness is the abode of the Dào;
even simplicity is the substance of the Dào;
clarity and tranquility are the mirror of the Dào;
softness and weakness are the function of the Dào.
Reversion is the constancy of the Dào;
softness is the firmness of the Dào;
weakness is the strength of the Dào.
Purity, plainness, and lack of adornment are the trunk of the Dào.
Emptiness means the center bears no burden;
evenness means the mind has no worries;
when desires and cravings bear no burden,
that is the ultimate emptiness;
when there are no likes or dislikes,
that is the ultimate evenness;
when unified and unchanging,
that is the ultimate tranquility;
when not mixed with external things,
that is the ultimate purity;
when neither sorrowful nor joyful,
that is the ultimate virtue.
Now, the rule of the ultimate person
discards cleverness,
extinguishes ornamentation,
relies on the Dào and abolishes wisdom,
sharing with the people in emerging from public-mindedness.
They restrict what they guard,
reduce what they seek,
remove enticements and desires,
eliminate cravings and wants,
diminish thoughts and worries.
Restricting what they guard brings clarity;
reducing what they seek brings attainment.
Thus, controlling the external from within,
no task is neglected;
gaining within, they can shepherd without.
When the center is attained,
the five viscera are calm,
thoughts and worries are even,
sinews and bones are strong,
ears and eyes are sharp.
The great Dào is level and broad,
not far from oneself.
Those who seek it far away
will go and yet return."
Lǎozǐ said:
The sage forgets about governing others,
but focuses on self-governance.
The noble forgets about power and status,
but seeks self-attainment;
with self-attainment, the world attains me.
Joy forgets about wealth and honor,
but resides in harmony.
Knowing to magnify the self and minimize the world
approaches the Dào.
Thus it is said:
"Attain the utmost emptiness,
maintain steadfast tranquility.
All things arise together,
and I thereby observe their return."
Now the Dào
molds and transforms all beings,
formless in beginning and end,
silent and unmoving,
vastly penetrating the obscure and dark.
So profoundly expansive it cannot be bounded externally,
so finely divided it cannot be contained internally.
It has no confined space,
yet gives rise to the collective names of being and non-being.
The zhēnrén embodies it through emptiness and nothingness,
simplicity,
clarity and tranquility,
softness and weakness,
purity and plainness—
not entangled with things,
ultimately attaining the Dào of heaven and earth.
Therefore called zhēnrén.
The zhēnrén
magnifies the self and minimizes the world,
values governing the self and disdains governing others,
not allowing things to disrupt harmony,
not allowing desires to disturb emotions.
Concealing name and surname,
when the Dào prevails, remains hidden;
when the Dào is absent, appears.
Acts without acting,
engages without engaging,
knows without knowing.
Embracing the great Dào,
encompassing the heart of heaven,
breathing yīn and yáng,
exhaling the old and inhaling the new,
closing with yīn,
opening with yáng,
rolling and unrolling with firmness and softness,
bending and rising with yīn and yáng,
sharing the heart of heaven,
becoming one with the Dào.
Without specific joys,
without specific sorrows,
without specific delights,
without specific angers—
all things mysteriously unified,
neither wrong nor right.
Now, when the body is harmed by the harshness of cold, heat, dryness, or dampness,
the body may wither but the spirit remains strong;
when the spirit is injured by the afflictions of joy, anger, thought, or worry,
the spirit may be exhausted while the body remains.
Thus, the zhēnrén uses the mind
to restore nature and rely on the spirit,
mutually supporting to achieve continuity.
Hence, they sleep without dreams,
and wake without worries.
Kǒngzǐ asked about the Dào.
Lǎozǐ said:
Straighten your form,
unify your gaze,
and heavenly harmony will arrive.
Gather your knowledge,
rectify your measure,
and the spirit will come to dwell.
Virtue will be your demeanor,
the Dào will be your abode.
Be wide-eyed,
like a newborn calf,
seeking no past causes.
Form like a withered tree,
mind like dead ashes—
truly knowing yet not clinging to cunning artifice,
vast and mindless, beyond plotting.
"Understanding clearly in all directions,
can there be no knowledge?"
Lǎozǐ said:
Those who handle affairs act in response to change,
change arises from timing,
and those who know timing have no constant actions.
Therefore,
"The Dào that can be spoken
is not the eternal Dào;
the name that can be named
is not the eternal name."
Writing arises from speech,
speech comes from wisdom,
but wisdom that knows not
is not the eternal Dào.
Names that can be named
are not for hoarding writings.
"Much learning leads to exhaustion,
better to hold to the center."
"Cease learning, and have no worries."
"Abandon sageliness, discard wisdom,
and the people will benefit a hundredfold."
Humans are born tranquil—
this is heaven's nature.
Stirred by things, they act—
this is nature's desire.
Responding as things arrive—
this is wisdom's movement.
likes and dislikes arise.
When likes and dislikes take form,
and wisdom emerges outwardly,
unable to return to oneself,
then heavenly principle perishes.
Thus, the sage does not replace heaven with human,
externally transforming with things while internally not losing true emotion.
Therefore, those who comprehend the Dào
return to clarity and tranquility;
those who investigate things
end in non-action.
Nourishing wisdom with calm,
uniting spirit with detachment,
approaching without gates,
following heaven is to wander with the Dào;
following humans is to interact with customs.
Hence, the sage does not let affairs disrupt heaven,
nor desires disturb emotions.
Without planning, yet appropriate;
without speaking, yet trustworthy;
without deliberating, yet attaining;
without acting, yet accomplishing.
Thus, residing above, the people feel no burden;
leading ahead, others cause no harm.
The world returns to them,
treachery and evil fear them.
Because they contend with nothing in the world,
none dare contend with them.
Lǎozi said:
When humans follow desires and lose their nature,
their actions are never correct.
Using this to govern a state brings chaos,
using this to cultivate oneself brings defilement.
Therefore, those who have not heard the Dào
have no means to return to their nature;
those who are not in harmony with things
cannot attain clarity and tranquility.
Originally, human nature is without evil or defilement;
long immersion in material things causes change,
and change that makes one forget their origin leads to conformity with a seeming nature.
Water's nature desires clarity,
but sand and stones defile it;
human nature desires peace,
but cravings and desires harm it.
Only the sage can discard things and return to oneself.
Thus, the sage does not use cleverness to control things,
nor let desires disrupt harmony.
In joy, they are not overly excited;
in sorrow, they are not deeply distressed.
Therefore, they are high without peril,
stable without collapse.
Thus, when hearing good words and expedient plans,
even the foolish know to appreciate them;
when praising sage-like virtue and lofty conduct,
even the unworthy know to admire them.
But those who appreciate are many, while those who apply are few;
those who admire are numerous, while those who practice are scarce.
The reason for this
is being tethered to things and bound by customs.
Hence it is said:
"I take no action, and the people transform themselves;
I prefer non-interference, and the people prosper themselves;
I love tranquility, and the people correct themselves;
I am without desire, and the people simplify themselves."
Clarity and tranquility are the pinnacle of virtue;
softness and weakness are the application of the Dào;
emptiness, nothingness, calmness, and contentment are the ancestors of all things.
When these three are practiced, one merges into the formless.
The formless
is called the One.
The One
is the mindless union with the world.
It spreads virtue without exhaustion,
functions without toil,
looked at but not seen,
listened to but not heard.
From the formless, forms are born;
from the silent, the five notes sound;
from the tasteless, the five flavors take shape;
from the colorless, the five colors are formed.
Thus, being is born from non-being,
the solid is born from the void.
The number of musical notes does not exceed five,
yet the variations of the five notes are more than can be heard;
the number of flavors does not exceed five,
yet the variations of the five flavors are more than can be tasted;
the number of colors does not exceed five,
yet the variations of the five colors are more than can be seen.
In sound, with the establishment of the gōng note, the five notes take form;
in taste, with the establishment of sweetness, the five flavors are determined;
in color, with the establishment of white, the five colors are completed;
in the Dào, with the establishment of the One, all things are born.
Therefore, the principle of the One
extends throughout the four seas;
the influence of the One
is observed between heaven and earth.
In its wholeness,
it is sincere, as if unhewn wood;
in its dispersion,
it is murky, as if turbid.
Turbid, yet gradually clears;
hollow, yet gradually fills.
Serene like the great sea,
expansive like floating clouds—
as if non-existent, yet present;
as if perished, yet surviving.
Lǎozi said:
The totality of all things
passes through a single aperture;
the roots of all affairs
emerge from a single gate.
Therefore, the sage follows a single standard and tracks the path,
not altering what is ancient,
not changing what is constant,
relying on the square and following the line,
adapting flexibly according to the constant.
Now, joy and anger
are deviations of the Dào;
worry and sorrow
are losses of virtue;
likes and dislikes
are faults of the heart;
cravings and desires
are burdens to life.
In humans, great anger damages the yīn,
great joy disrupts the yáng;
weak energy causes muteness,
fright and fear lead to madness;
worry, sorrow, and anxiety
cause illnesses to accumulate.
If one can eliminate these five,
they then unite with divine clarity.
Divine clarity
is attained internally;
those who attain it internally
have tranquil five organs,
calm thoughts and considerations,
keen ears and clear eyes,
strong sinews and bones,
penetrating understanding without confusion,
firm and strong without exhaustion,
never excessive in anything,
and nothing beyond their reach.
Nothing in the world is softer and weaker than water,
yet the way of water
is broad beyond limits,
deep beyond measure,
long without end,
distant and vast without shores.
Its decrease and increase,
surpass the incalculable.
In heaven, it becomes rain and dew;
on earth, it becomes moisture and nourishment.
All things cannot but grow because of it;
all affairs cannot but be accomplished because of it.
It greatly embraces all living beings without private preferences,
its moisture reaches even the smallest insects without seeking reward,
it enriches the world without exhaustion,
its virtue benefits the common people without cost.
Its movement cannot be grasped and exhausted;
its subtlety cannot be held in hand.
Strike it, and it shows no wound;
stab it, and it incurs no injury;
chop it, and it is not severed;
burn it, and it is not scorched.
Soft and flowing, it follows its course and cannot be scattered;
its sharpness penetrates metal and stone;
its strength aids the world.
Whether in surplus or deficiency,
it lets the world take and give freely;
receiving and bearing all things without preference or sequence,
without private or public bias,
it merges with heaven and earth in vast unity.
This is called the ultimate virtue.
The reason water can achieve its ultimate virtue
is its softness, moisture, and smoothness.
Hence it is said:
"The softest thing in the world
gallops through the hardest thing in the world.
The non-existent enters the seamless."
Now, the formless
is the great ancestor of things;
the soundless
is the great ancestor of categories.
The true person
is one whose essence connects with the spiritual storehouse,
who companions with the creator of transformations,
holding profound virtue in the heart,
and transforming with divine speed.
Therefore, the Dào that is not spoken of as Dào
is vast and magnificent!
Without issuing commands or orders, yet able to shift customs and change habits—
this is only possible through the action of the heart.
All things have their origin, yet only they know to guard the root;
all affairs have their source, yet only they know to guard the gate.
Thus, they can exhaust the inexhaustible,
reach the unreachable,
illuminate things without being dazzled,
respond like an echo without conscious effort.
Lǎo zǐ said:
Those who attain the Dào,
have pliant wills yet accomplish strongly,
with empty minds they respond fittingly.
A pliant will is soft, yielding, tranquil, and quiet,
hiding in what one dares not,
acting in what one cannot,
serenely without action,
moving without missing the timing.
Hence,
"Nobility must take humility as its root,
height must take lowness as its foundation."
Entrusting the small to encompass the great,
being within to control the outer,
acting softly yet being firm,
their strength is unconquerable,
no enemy is not overcome,
responding to change and assessing the time,
none can harm them.
Those who wish to be firm must guard it with softness,
those who wish to be strong must preserve it with weakness.
Accumulate softness and it becomes firm,
accumulate weakness and it becomes strength.
Observe what is accumulated,
to know survival or demise.
Strength overcomes those not equal to oneself,
but meets its match against equals;
softness overcomes those surpassing oneself,
its power is immeasurable.
Hence,
"When weapons are strong, they are destroyed;
when trees are strong, they are broken."
When leather is strong, it splits;
teeth are harder than the tongue but wear out first.
Therefore,
"The soft and weak are the trunk of life,
the hard and strong are the companions of death."
Leading first is the path to exhaustion,
acting later is the source of attainment.
Holding the Dào to couple with change,
the first can control the last,
the last can also control the first.
Why so?
Not losing the means to control others,
others cannot control one either.
What is called 'later'
adjusts its measure and aligns with the timing.
The turning of time
allows not a moment's pause;
to act too early is excessive,
to act too late falls short.
The sun revolves, the moon cycles,
time does not linger with man.
Thus the sage does not value a foot-long jade,
but values an inch of time,
for time is hard to gain and easy to lose.
Therefore, the sage acts according to the time,
achieves merit based on resources,
guards the clear Dào,
restrains the feminine node,
follows along and responds to change,
often staying behind and not leading,
soft and weak to be tranquil,
peaceful and gradual to be stable.
Their great merit crushes the坚固,
none can contend with them.
Lǎo zǐ said:
If a mechanical heart is hidden within,
then purity and whiteness are not refined,
spiritual virtue is incomplete.
If one does not know what is in oneself,
how can one embrace what is far?
If harmful intentions are forgotten within,
even a hungry tiger can be followed,
let alone humans.
Those who embody the Dào are at ease and never exhausted,
those who rely on cunning labor without achievement.
Laws that are harsh and punishments that execute
are not the enterprise of emperors and kings;
frequent use of whips and prods
is not the driving for long distances.
Excessive likes and dislikes
bring disaster in their wake.
Thus the laws of the former kings were not created,
but inherited;
their prohibitions and executions were not enacted,
but upheld.
Hence, being able to inherit leads to greatness,
creating leads to pettiness;
being able to uphold leads to solidity,
acting leads to failure.
Relying on ears and eyes to hear and see
tires the mind without clarity;
using intellect and scheming to manage affairs
torments the heart without achievement.
Relying on one person's talent is难以达到治理,
one person's ability is insufficient to manage a three-acre homestead.
Following the principles of the Dào,
according to heaven and earth's natural state,
even the six directions are not enough to balance.
Hearing lost in slander and praise,
eyes indulging in colors,
rituals are insufficient to prevent attachment,
sincere heart can embrace the distant.
Thus no weapon is more cruel than the will,
and Mò Yé is inferior;
no invader is greater than yīn and yáng,
and war drums are minor.
The so-called great invaders lie silent with corpses,
medium invaders hide in mountains,
small invaders hide among the people.
Hence it is said:
"When the people have much wisdom and cunning,
bizarre things proliferate;
when laws and decrees multiply,
thieves and robbers abound."
Discard that and take this,
and heaven's calamities will not arise.
"Thus governing a state with wisdom
is the state's thief;
governing a state without wisdom
is the state's virtue."
The formless is great,
the formed is small;
the formless is abundant,
the formed is scarce;
the formless is strong,
the formed is weak;
the formless is substantial,
the formed is empty.
The formed completes affairs,
the formless initiates beginnings.
Completed affairs become vessels,
initiated beginnings are the uncarved block.
The formed has sound,
the formless has no sound;
the formed is produced from the formless,
thus the formless is the beginning of the formed.
Broad and thick have names,
having names is valued and complete;
frugal and thin are nameless,
being nameless is despised and轻;
wealthy and abundant have names,
having names is honored and favored;
poor and scarce are nameless,
being nameless is lowly and humiliated;
male and virile have names,
having names manifest virtue;
female and receptive are nameless,
being nameless is hidden and obscure;
surplus has names,
having names is exalted and worthy;
deficiency is nameless,
being nameless is entrusted to the lower;
having merit means having a name,
lacking merit means being nameless;
names are produced from the nameless,
the nameless is the mother of names.
The Dào,
"being and non-being generate each other,
difficult and easy complete each other."
Therefore, the sage holds the Dào in emptiness and tranquility,
subtle and marvelous to complete their virtue.
Thus having the Dào means having virtue,
having virtue means having merit,
having merit means having a name,
having a name means returning again to the Dào.
Merit and fame endure long,
lifelong without blame.
Kings and dukes have merit and fame,
the solitary and widowed have no merit or fame.
Hence it is said:
"The sage calls themselves solitary and widowed."
Returning to their root and origin,
achieving merit without possessing it.
Thus having merit is considered benefit,
being nameless is considered usefulness.
In ancient times, people were childlike and ignorant,
not knowing east from west,
appearance not separated from true nature,
words not exceeding actions,
actions without posturing,
speaking without ornamentation.
Their clothes provided warmth without color,
their weapons were blunt without edges.
They walked steadily,
gazed vacantly,
dug wells to drink,
plowed fields to eat,
did not give alms,
did not seek virtue.
High and low did not topple each other,
long and short did not compare.
Customs aligned with the wind could be followed,
affairs suited to ability were easy to do.
Boasting and falsity to deceive the world,
eccentric conduct to confuse the masses—
the sage does not consider these as people's customs.
Lǎozǐ said:
Heaven achieves its height,
Earth achieves its depth,
the sun and moon shine,
the stars gleam,
Yīn and Yáng harmonize—
not by deliberate action,
but by aligning with the Dào, whereby things follow their natural course.
Yīn, Yáng, and the four seasons do not intentionally generate all things;
rain and dew fall in season not to nourish plants and trees;
rather, when divine intelligence connects,
and Yīn and Yáng harmonize,
all things come to life.
Now, the Dào
stores essence within,
dwells with spirit in the heart,
in stillness, tranquility, and simplicity,
serene within the breast,
vast and formless,
silent and soundless.
Thus, government offices seem as if without affairs,
the court as if without people;
there are no recluses,
no hermits,
no forced labor,
no unjust punishments.
All under heaven look up to the ruler's virtue,
emulating the sovereign's intent.
Distant lands with different customs all send interpreters and come,
not because the ruler visits each household,
but because his sincere heart
extends throughout the world.
Thus, rewarding the good and punishing the violent
are matters of governance;
but what enables their implementation
is sincere essence.
Decrees may be clear but cannot act alone;
they must await sincere essence.
Hence, if one governs the people with the Dào yet they do not follow,
it is because sincere essence has not arrived.
Lǎozǐ said:
Heaven establishes the sun and moon,
arrays the stars,
spreads out the four seasons,
and harmonizes Yīn and Yáng.
By day, it dries things;
by night, it lets them rest;
by wind, it desiccates;
by rain and dew, it moistens.
In generating things,
none see how they are nurtured, yet all things grow;
in destroying things,
none see how they are lost, yet all things perish.
This is called divine intelligence.
Therefore, the sage emulates this:
when he brings forth blessings,
none see the means, yet blessings arise;
when he removes calamities,
none see the method, yet calamities vanish.
Seek it, and it cannot be grasped;
examine it, and it is not empty.
Daily calculations fall short,
but yearly calculations yield surplus.
Silent and soundless,
one word can greatly move the world—
this is how the heart of Heaven stirs transformation.
Thus, when sincere essence takes form within,
its energy moves Heaven,
auspicious stars appear,
yellow dragons descend,
phoenixes arrive,
sweet springs emerge,
excellent grains grow,
rivers do not overflow,
seas do not surge.
But acting against Heaven and harming things
brings eclipses of the sun and moon,
the five planets stray from their courses,
the four seasons conflict,
daylight dims and night glows,
mountains collapse and rivers run dry,
winter thunders and summer frosts.
Heaven and humanity
are interconnected;
thus, when a state declines and falls,
celestial patterns change,
worldly customs chaos,
rainbows appear.
All things are interconnected;
essential energies influence each other.
Therefore, affairs of divine intelligence
cannot be achieved by cleverness or artifice,
nor forced by strength.
Hence, the great person unites in virtue with Heaven and Earth,
in brightness with the sun and moon,
in spirituality with ghosts and gods,
in trustworthiness with the four seasons.
Embracing the heart of Heaven,
holding the energy of Earth,
grasping emptiness and containing harmony,
they act throughout the four seas without leaving the hall,
transform customs,
and guide the people to change for the better,
as if it came from themselves—
this is the ability to transform through spirit.
Lǎozǐ said:
As for the way of humanity,
it preserves nature and protects authenticity,
not harming the self.
When encountering urgency or adversity,
one's essence connects with Heaven.
If one never departs from their origin,
what can they not accomplish?
Death and life share the same realm,
and cannot be threatened or coerced;
how much more so for one who governs Heaven and Earth,
stores all things,
befriends creation,
and contains ultimate harmony—
such a one has never truly died.
When sincere essence forms within,
it is understood by others' hearts without—
this is the untransmittable Dào.
When a sage is in position above,
they embrace the Dào without speaking,
yet their grace reaches all people.
Thus, the teaching without words
is vast and magnificent!
If ruler and minister are at odds,
deception appears in Heaven,
and spiritual energies respond accordingly—
this is a clear sign.
This is called the unspoken argument,
the unstated Dào.
To summon the distant, employ non-action;
to draw the near, speak of non-interference.
Only those who walk in darkness can possess this.
Thus, racehorses are retired to manure fields,
and chariot tracks do not reach distant lands—
this is called sitting still while racing, sinking on land.
The Dào of Heaven shows no partiality in drawing near,
nor in departing;
the capable have surplus,
the inept have lack.
Those who follow it gain benefit;
those who oppose it meet misfortune.
Therefore, those who rule by cleverness find it hard to sustain the state;
only those who unite with the great harmony and hold to natural responses
can achieve it.
Lǎozǐ said:
The relationship between Dào and Dé
is like that between leather and hide—
distant, yet near;
near, yet distant.
Seek it, and it cannot be grasped;
examine it, and it is not empty.
Therefore, the sage is like a mirror:
neither sending nor welcoming,
responding without storing,
transforming with all things yet unharmed.
What is gained
is also lost;
what is lost
is also gained.
Thus, those who penetrate the great harmony
are like one deeply drunk, sweetly asleep, roaming within it,
as if never having left their origin.
This is called great penetration,
whereby the unused enables the use.
Lǎo zǐ said:
In ancient times, when Huángdì ruled the world,
he harmonized the movements of the sun and moon,
regulated the energies of yīn and yáng,
moderated the measures of the four seasons,
corrected the calculations of pitch standards and calendars,
distinguished male from female,
clarified superior and subordinate,
ensuring the strong did not oppress the weak,
the many did not brutalize the few,
the people preserved their lives without premature death,
the harvests were ripe without calamity,
officials were upright and without selfishness,
superiors and subordinates were harmonious without fault,
laws and decrees were clear and not obscure,
assistants were impartial and not flattering,
farmers yielded field boundaries,
lost items were not picked up on the road,
markets required no haggling over prices.
Thus, at that time,
the sun, moon, and stars did not stray from their courses,
wind and rain came in due season,
the five grains were abundant and flourishing,
the phoenix soared in the courtyards,
the qílín roamed in the suburbs.
When Fúxī shì ruled the world,
he used a stone for a pillow and a rope for a bed,
restrained himself in autumn and winter,
bore the square earth,
embraced the round heaven,
unblocked what was obstructed and stagnant in the yīn and yáng,
and halted what perverse energies, harmful things, and hoarding that injured the people.
He stopped them completely.
His people were innocent, knowing not east from west,
gazing blankly,
walking unsteadily,
content in their simplicity,
unaware of their origins,
drifting aimlessly,
not knowing their roots,
nourishing themselves without knowing where to go.
At that time,
beasts, insects, and snakes all concealed their claws and fangs,
hid their venom and stings,
achieving merits that matched heaven and earth.
When Huángdì reached the essence under the Great Ancestor,
yet he did not display his achievements,
did not proclaim his fame,
concealing the way of the true person,
to follow the natural course of heaven and earth.
Why so?
Because his virtue and way connected with the highest,
and cunning intellect was eliminated.
Lǎo zǐ said:
If heaven is unsettled,
the sun and moon have nothing to rely on;
if earth is unsettled,
plants and trees have nothing to stand on;
if the body is unquiet,
right and wrong have no form.
Thus, only with a true person is there true knowledge.
If what one holds is unclear,
how can I know that what I call knowing is not ignorance?
Accumulating kindness and heavy bribes,
making the people joyful,
so that they delight in life—
this is benevolence.
Achieving great merits,
displaying a good name,
ordering ruler and minister with propriety,
rectifying superior and subordinate,
clarifying closeness and distance,
preserving endangered states,
continuing extinct lineages,
establishing heirs for those without—
this is righteousness.
Closing the nine orifices,
concealing will and intent,
discarding cleverness,
returning to无知,
wandering freely beyond the dust and grime,
roaming carefree in the realm of non-action,
embracing yīn and exhaling yáng, harmonizing with all things—
this is virtue.
Thus, the Way scatters and becomes virtue,
virtue overflows and becomes benevolence and righteousness,
and when benevolence and righteousness are established, the Way and virtue are abandoned.
Lǎo zǐ said:
When the spirit is distracted, speech becomes flowery;
when virtue is dissipated, conduct becomes false.
If the utmost essence is lost within,
then speech and action are observed outwardly,
this unavoidably enslaves the self to things.
When essence is depleted but actions are endless,
what is held within is unstable and one is excessively influenced by worldly customs.
Therefore, the sage cultivates the Way and virtue inwardly without outwardly adorning with benevolence and righteousness,
knows the proper use of the nine orifices and four limbs,
and wanders in the harmony of spirit and essence—
this is the wandering of the sage.
Lǎo zǐ said:
As for the wandering of the sage,
it moves in the utmost emptiness,
the heart roams in great nothingness,
galloping beyond the confines,
walking where there is no gate,
listening to the soundless,
gazing at the formless,
unconstrained by the world,
untied by customs.
Thus, what the worthy use to move the world,
the true person does not pass;
what the virtuous use to correct customs,
the sage does not observe.
If a person is constrained by worldly customs,
the body is bound and the spirit leaks,
thus unavoidably burdened.
If I can be bound,
it must be that my fate has external attachments.
Lǎo zǐ said:
When the thoughts of a ruler
do not let the spirit gallop in the chest,
nor let wisdom extend beyond the four domains,
but embrace a heart of sincere benevolence,
then sweet rain falls in season,
the five grains multiply and grow,
spring births, summer matures,
autumn harvests, winter stores,
with monthly inspections and seasonal assessments,
ending the year with tributes offered;
nourishing the people with fairness,
authority stern but not tested,
laws simple and not burdensome,
teaching transformative like divinity,
regulations lenient, punishments relaxed,
prisons empty and void,
the world unified in custom,
none harboring deceitful hearts—
this is the grace of the sage.
If those above are fond of taking without limit,
then those below become greedy for merit without yielding,
the people impoverished and contentious,
laboring hard without achievement,
cunning and deceit sprouting,
thieves and robbers proliferating,
superiors and subordinates resentful,
commands unenforceable.
When water is turbid, fish gasp;
when governance is harsh, the people rebel.
If the ruler has many desires, the people become deceitful;
if the ruler is overly meddlesome, the people become unsettled;
if the ruler seeks much, the people contend with each other.
Not governing the root but rescuing the branches
is no different from digging a channel to stop water
or carrying firewood to extinguish a fire.
The sage's affairs are few and easy to govern,
his demands scant and easy to satisfy,
bestowing kindness without acting,
trusted without speaking,
gaining without seeking,
succeeding without doing,
embracing spontaneity,
preserving utmost truth,
holding the Way and extending sincerity,
the world follows him like an echo responding to a sound,
a shadow resembling a form—
for what he cultivates is the root.
Lǎo zǐ said:
When spirit and essence stray outward,
and wisdom and thoughts churn inwardly,
one cannot govern the form.
The farther the spirit is used,
the nearer what is neglected.
Hence,
"Without going out the door, one knows the world;
without peering through the window, one knows the heavenly Way.
The farther one goes,
the less one knows."
This means that essence and sincerity emanate from within,
and spirit and energy move in accord with heaven.
Lǎozǐ said:
The winter sun,
the summer shade,
all things return to them without being directed,
the ultimate natural and most refined influence,
arrives unsummoned,
departs unbanished,
profound and obscure,
without knowing how it acts, yet achievements form naturally;
to rely on eyes for illumination,
or on words to issue commands,
makes governance difficult indeed.
Gāo Yáo, though mute, served as Chief Justice,
and the world had no cruel punishments—
what need was there for words?
Shī Kuàng, though blind, served as Grand Steward,
and the state of Jìn had no chaotic governance—
what need was there for sight?
Commands without words,
vision without looking,
are what the sage uses as his guide.
The people's transformation by their superiors
follows not their words but their actions.
Thus, if a ruler favors bravery,
even without ordering fights, the state will face many troubles;
gradually, plunder and murder will arise.
If a ruler favors beauty,
even without permitting gossip, the state will fall into disorder;
accumulatively, it will lead to the calamity of debauchery.
Therefore, the sage embodies essential sincerity within,
and makes likes and dislikes clear without,
speaking words that match his feelings,
issuing decrees that clarify his intent.
Hence, punishments are insufficient to change customs,
executions inadequate to stop wickedness;
only spiritual transformation is valued.
The ultimate essence is spiritual;
when essence moves,
it is like the growth of spring's energy,
or the withering of autumn's energy.
Thus, the ruler of men
is like an archer:
a hair's breadth here
makes a vast difference there!
So, one who governs people
must be cautious about what influences them.
Lǎozǐ said:
To hang laws and set rewards yet fail to change customs and practices
is due to a lack of sincere heart.
Thus, hearing the music reveals the customs,
observing the music shows the practices,
seeing the practices indicates the transformation.
Those who embrace truth and manifest sincerity
move heaven and earth,
influence realms beyond,
enacting orders and prohibitions effectively.
By sincerely connecting with the Dào and conveying its intent,
even without a single word,
all people under heaven,
beasts,
and spirits transform with it.
Therefore, the highest is spiritual transformation,
next is preventing wrongdoing,
lowest is rewarding the worthy and punishing the violent.
Lǎozǐ said:
The great Dào is non-action,
non-action means non-being,
non-being does not dwell,
not dwelling means residing without form,
formless means motionless,
motionless means wordless,
wordless means tranquil and soundless.
Without form or sound,
it cannot be seen when looked at,
cannot be heard when listened to;
this is called subtle and mysterious,
this is called supremely spiritual,
"continuous, as if ever-present,"
"this is called the root of heaven and earth."
The Dào has no form or sound,
so the sage forcibly gives it form,
using one word as its name:
the Dào of heaven and earth.
The great takes the small as its basis,
the many begins with the few.
The Son of Heaven takes heaven and earth as his model,
the myriad things as his resources;
his merit and virtue are utmost great,
his power and name utmost noble.
The beauty of these two virtues matches heaven and earth,
so he must follow the great Dào as the mother of all under heaven.
Lǎozǐ said:
Relieving poverty and aiding the urgent gives rise to fame,
promoting benefits and removing harms accomplishes merit.
If the world has no disasters,
even a sage has no virtue to display;
if above and below are harmonious,
even a worthy has no merit to establish.
Thus, the rule of the ultimate person
embodies virtue and embraces the Dào,
extends sincerity and delights in giving,
holding boundless wisdom,
resting in persuasion without words.
None under heaven know to value his wordlessness,
hence
"the Dào that can be spoken
is not the eternal Dào;
the name that can be named
is not the eternal name."
What is recorded on bamboo and silk,
engraved on metal and stone,
and can be passed to others
is all coarse.
The Three Sovereigns, Five Emperors, and Three Kings
differed in affairs but shared the same heart,
took different paths but reached the same end.
Later age learners,
not knowing the Dào's unified substance,
or virtue's essential summary,
take the traces of accomplished deeds,
kneel and sit to discuss them;
though learned and knowledgeable,
they cannot avoid confusion.
Lǎozǐ said:
The essence of the heart
can spiritually transform,
but cannot be conveyed in words.
The sage does not leave his mat yet rectifies the world,
his emotion more effective than shouting.
Thus, when he speaks, the people trust him—
trust precedes the words;
when he commands, they act—
sincerity lies beyond the command.
When the sage is above,
the people transform as if by spirit,
emotion leading the way.
If actions above get no response below,
it's because emotion and command differ.
A three-month infant knows not benefit or harm,
yet a loving mother's care reaches it—
this is emotion.
Thus, the use of words causes change,
but the change is small;
the use of wordlessness causes change,
and the change is great.
Trustworthiness is the gentleman's words,
loyalty is the gentleman's intent;
with loyalty and trust within,
movement and response occur without—
this is the transformation of sages and worthies.
Lǎozǐ said:
A son dying for his father,
a minister dying for his ruler—
not done to seek fame,
but because kindness hidden within does not shun hardship.
The gentleman's grief is not for show,
it comes from within.
Observe also one's nightly conduct;
the sage feels no shame before his shadow,
the gentleman is cautious when alone.
To discard the near for the distant
is blockage.
Thus, with the sage above, the people delight in his rule;
with him below, they admire his intent,
never forgetting his desire to benefit others.
Lǎozǐ said:
A brave warrior's single shout
makes the whole army yield—
such is the sincerity of its emission.
To lead without harmony,
intend without support,
means the heart must have some discord.
Not leaving his mat yet rectifying the world,
he seeks it within himself.
Thus, where persuasion fails to reach,
appearance reaches;
where appearance fails to reach,
subtle influence reaches.
Moved in the heart, it manifests in form;
the ultimate essence can connect through form,
but cannot be scheduled like illumination.
Lǎozi said:
Words have their source,
affairs have their root.
If one loses their source and root,
even with many skills,
it is better to have few.
The Zhou tripod depicted Chuí yet had his fingers cut off,
to show that great cleverness should not be practiced.
Thus, a craftsman's wisdom in action
does not rely on ability alone but on timing.
To close without knowing how to close,
one must first block before opening.
Lǎozi said:
The sage's engagement in affairs
follows different paths but reaches the same end,
preserving life and stabilizing collapse as one,
his mind never forgetting the desire to benefit others.
Thus, the songs of Qín, Chǔ, Yān, and Wèi
differ in sound but all bring joy;
the cries of the nine Yí and eight Dí tribes
differ in sound but all express sorrow.
For singing is a sign of joy,
crying an effect of grief.
What is harbored within
emanates outward;
thus, it depends on what moves it.
The sage's heart,
day and night, never forgets the desire to benefit others,
and the reach of his influence is far indeed.
Lǎozi said:
One governs through non-action,
for action leads to harm.
Governing through non-action
means acting without action;
those who act cannot achieve non-action.
Those who cannot achieve non-action
cannot truly act either.
One is spiritual without words,
for words lead to harm.
Being spiritual without words
means carrying emptiness;
otherwise, it harms the spirit that possesses spirituality.
Wénzǐ said:
Fame can be forcefully established,
achievements can be forcefully accomplished.
In the past, Nán Róng Chú felt ashamed of the sagely way and alone lost himself,
went south to see Lǎozi,
received a single teaching,
his spirit and essence became clear and luminous,
blockages opened and pathways smoothed,
enduring hardship for ten days without eating,
as if enjoying a grand sacrifice.
Thus, his brilliance illuminated all within the seas,
his fame established for later generations,
his wisdom connected heaven and earth,
his discernment distinguished the finest details,
praises and elegant words
continue unceasing to this day.
This is what is called fame that can be forcefully established.
Thus, if farmers do not exert themselves,
granaries will not be full;
if officials are not diligent,
sincerity will not be refined;
if generals and ministers do not strive,
merits and deeds will not be achieved;
if kings and nobles are negligent,
later generations will have no renown.
The perfect person moves unseen,
like thunder hidden away,
acting in accordance with the time,
achieving success based on resources,
advancing or retreating without difficulty,
unobstructed in all things.
For the perfect person's essence and sincerity take form within,
his virtue flows to the four directions;
seeing benefit in the world,
he rejoices and does not forget;
seeing harm in the world,
he is alarmed as if suffering a loss.
"Those who worry about the people's worries,
the people will also worry about their worries;
those who rejoice in the people's joys,
the people will also rejoice in their joys.
Thus, worrying for the world,
rejoicing for the world,
yet not becoming king—
such a thing has never happened."
"The sage's methods
begin with what cannot be seen,
end with what cannot be reached,
reside in unshakable ground,
accumulate in inexhaustible granaries,
are stored in unfailing treasuries;
issuing commands like the source of flowing water,
employing the people in non-contentious roles,
opening gates that ensure gain,
not attempting what cannot be accomplished,
not seeking what cannot be obtained,
not dwelling where one cannot last,
not practicing what cannot be repeated."
The great man implements governance that pleases,
and none disobey his commands;
if commands are agreeable, they are followed,
small efforts leading to great results;
if commands are contrary, good turns to harm,
success becomes failure.
What is called a great man
is strong within and bright without;
strong within like heaven and earth,
bright without like the sun and moon.
Heaven and earth cover and carry all,
the sun and moon illuminate all.
The great man shows goodness to others,
unchanging in his ways,
unshifting in his constancy;
the world obeys his orders
like grass bending to the wind.
If governance fails in spring,
Jupiter expands or contracts,
not staying in its usual course;
if governance fails in summer,
Mars retrogresses;
if governance fails in autumn,
Venus is misplaced,
appearing and disappearing irregularly;
if governance fails in winter,
Mercury does not appear in its proper quarter;
if governance fails in all four seasons,
Saturn shakes and wanders,
the sun and moon show reproach,
the five planets rebel in chaos,
comets appear.
If spring governance does not fail, grains flourish;
if summer governance does not fail, rain falls timely;
if autumn governance does not fail, the people prosper;
if winter governance does not fail, the state is peaceful and healthy.
Lǎozi said:
Before heaven and earth took form,
all was deep and dark,
merged into one,
silent and clear,
the heavy and turbid became earth,
the refined and subtle became heaven.
Separating, they formed the four seasons;
dividing, they became yīn and yáng.
The essential qì became humans,
the coarse qì became insects.
Hard and soft complementing each other,
all things were born.
Spirit and essence originate from heaven,
bones and skeleton root in earth.
When spirit and essence enter their gate,
bones and skeleton return to their root,
what of me remains?
Thus, the sage emulates heaven and follows earth,
unconstrained by customs,
unswayed by others,
taking heaven as father,
earth as mother,
yīn and yáng as the guiding principles,
the four seasons as the framework.
Heaven, tranquil and clear;
earth, stable and peaceful.
Those who go against them perish,
those who follow them thrive.
Thus, stillness and silence are the abode of spirit and clarity,
emptiness and nothingness are where the Dào resides.
For spirit and essence are received from heaven,
bones and skeleton are endowed by earth.
"The Dào gives birth to the One,
the One gives birth to the Two,
the Two give birth to the Three,
the Three give birth to all things.
All things carry yīn and embrace yáng,
blending qì to achieve harmony."
Lǎozi said:
Humans are born through the transformations of heaven and earth:
in the first month, as a greasy substance;
in the second month, blood vessels form;
in the third month, as an embryo;
in the fourth month, as a fetus;
in the fifth month, tendons develop;
in the sixth month, bones form;
in the seventh month, the body takes shape;
in the eighth month, movement begins;
in the ninth month, restlessness occurs;
in the tenth month, birth happens.
The physical form is complete,
the five organs are divided,
the liver governs the eyes,
the lungs govern the nose,
the spleen governs the tongue,
the kidneys govern the ears,
the gallbladder governs the mouth,
the exterior serves as the surface,
the interior as the inner layer,
the head is round, modeling heaven,
the feet are square, symbolizing earth,
heaven has four seasons,
five phases,
nine luminaries, and three hundred sixty days,
humans have four limbs,
five organs,
nine orifices, and three hundred sixty joints.
Heaven has wind, rain, cold, and heat,
humans have taking, giving, joy, and anger,
the gallbladder is like clouds,
the lungs like qi,
the spleen like wind,
the kidneys like rain,
the liver like thunder,
humans are analogous to heaven and earth,
with the heart as their ruler;
the ears and eyes are the sun and moon,
blood and qi are the wind and rain,
if the sun and moon deviate from their course,
eclipses occur and they lose their light,
if wind and rain come at the wrong time,
destruction arises and disasters occur,
if the five planets stray from their paths,
states and regions suffer calamity.
The way of heaven and earth,
vast and grand,
still regulates its brilliance,
cherishes its divine light,
how can human ears and eyes be constantly stimulated without rest?
How can the spirit gallop without becoming weary?
Thus, the sage guards the inner without losing the outer.
Blood and qi are the bloom of a person,
the five organs are the essence of a person,
if blood and qi can concentrate within and not spill outward,
then the chest and abdomen are full and desires are few,
with few desires, the ears and eyes are clear, hearing and vision acute and penetrating,
acute hearing and vision are called clarity;
if the five organs can belong to the heart without separation,
then the will is strong and actions are not perverse,
the spirit is abundant and qi does not scatter,
so that hearing misses nothing,
vision overlooks nothing,
endeavors achieve everything,
calamities find no way in,
evil qi cannot assail;
thus, those who seek much gain little,
those who see grandly know little.
The orifices are the windows of the spirit,
blood and qi are the messengers of the five organs,
so if ears and eyes indulge in sounds and sights,
the five organs become agitated and unstable,
blood and qi surge and do not rest,
the spirit gallops and does not stay,
even if fortune and misfortune arrive like mountains,
there is no way to recognize them,
thus the sage cherishes and does not transgress.
The sage truly makes ears, eyes, and spirit profoundly penetrating,
without being seduced or enamored,
the will and qi remain clear and tranquil with few desires,
the five organs are thus at peace,
the spirit internally guards the form without transgression,
then one can observe beyond past ages,
within future events,
and fully perceive the interplay of fortune and misfortune,
hence
"the farther one goes out,
the less one knows."
This means the spirit must not be allowed to wander externally.
Therefore,
"the five colors confuse the eyes,
making them unclear,
the five sounds enter the ears,
making them unhearing,
the five flavors confuse the mouth,
causing it to develop sores,
choices and rejections disturb the heart,
making actions flighty,"
thus desires cause a person's qi to become excessive,
likes and dislikes cause the essence to toil,
if not quickly removed,
the will and qi daily diminish.
The reason people cannot live out their natural lifespan
is because they overly nourish life,
only those who do not act for the sake of life
thereby attain longevity,
heaven and earth move and interconnect,
all things unite as one,
to know the one is to know everything,
not to know the one is to know nothing.
I exist in the world as one thing,
and things are also things,
thing among things,
how can they judge each other?
Desire for life cannot be forced,
hatred of death cannot be avoided,
do not despise what is lowly,
do not rejoice in what is noble,
follow their nature and pacify them,
dare not go to extremes,
not going to extremes is the ultimate joy.
3.1. Guarding Emptiness One
Lǎozǐ said:
The so-called sage,
adapts to the times and is content in their position,
seizes the moment and enjoys their work,
for sorrow and joy are deviations of virtue,
likes and dislikes are burdens of the heart,
joy and anger are excesses of the way;
thus their life is a natural course,
their death is a transformation of things,
in stillness, they unite with the virtue of yīn,
in movement, they harmonize with the waves of yáng.
Hence, the heart is the master of the form,
the spirit is the treasure of the heart,
if the form labors without rest, it collapses,
if the essence is used without cease, it is exhausted,
therefore, the sage adheres to this and dares not transgress.
Responding to being with non-being,
one must investigate its principle,
receiving fullness with emptiness,
one must exhaust its details,
serene and content in emptiness and stillness,
to complete one's destiny,
neither alienating,
nor favoring,
embracing virtue and warming harmony,
to comply with heaven,
meeting with the way,
neighboring with virtue,
not initiating fortune,
not preceding misfortune,
death and life bring no change to oneself,
thus it is called supreme spirituality.
With spirituality, seeking finds all,
acting achieves all.
3.2. Guarding Non-being Two
Lǎozǐ said:
To regard the world lightly means the spirit is unburdened,
to view all things as small means the heart is unconfused,
to equalize life and death means the will is unafraid,
to identify with changes means clarity is undazzled.
The ultimate person leans on an unyielding pillar,
walks a path without barriers,
draws from an inexhaustible source,
learns from an undying teacher,
goes nowhere without success,
reaches nowhere without penetration,
bending and stretching, bowing and rising,
holding to destiny unconfused and adaptable,
fortune, misfortune, benefit, and harm,
are insufficient to trouble the heart.
Those who act for righteousness can be urged by benevolence,
but cannot be coerced by arms,
can be stopped by righteousness,
cannot be tempted by profit;
the noble person dies for righteousness,
cannot be detained by wealth and honor,
for righteousness, cannot be threatened by death,
how much more so for those who practice non-action!
Those who practice non-action are unburdened,
the unburdened person,
regards the world as a shadow pillar.
Observing above the principles of the ultimate person,
deeply tracing the meaning of the way and virtue,
examining below the behaviors of the世俗,
is enough to feel shame;
those who do not act for the sake of the world,
are like setting up a drum for learning.
3.3. Guarding Equanimity Three
Lǎozǐ said:
High status and great profit,
are what people covet,
compared to the self, they are base,
thus the sage eats only enough to fill emptiness and connect qi,
clothes only enough to cover the form and ward off cold,
satisfies emotions and rejects excess,
does not covet gain,
does not accumulate much,
clears the eyes to not see,
quiets the ears to not hear,
closes the mouth to not speak,
entrusts the heart to not ponder,
Discard cleverness,
return to pristine simplicity,
rest your vital essence and spirit,
eliminate knowledge and artifice,
have no likes or dislikes,
this is called the Great Pervasion.
To remove defilements and burdens,
nothing compares to never departing from your ancestral source,
then what undertaking would not succeed?
Those who understand the harmony of nurturing life
cannot be tempted by profit,
those who comprehend the correspondence between inner and outer
cannot be seduced by power.
The unbounded beyond boundaries
is the ultimate greatness,
the core within the coreless
is the ultimate nobility.
Being able to know this great nobility,
wherever one goes, nothing fails to proceed.
3.4. Central Harmony Four
Lǎozi said:
Those in ancient times who practiced the Dào
regulated their emotions and nature,
cultivated their mental dispositions,
nourished themselves with harmony,
maintained themselves with moderation,
delighted in the Dào and forgot their lowly status,
rested in virtue and forgot their poverty.
When their nature had no desires,
there were no desires unfulfilled;
when their minds had no pleasures,
there were no pleasures not realized.
What does not benefit their nature, they do not allow to burden their virtue;
what does not facilitate life, they do not allow to disrupt harmony. Not indulging their bodies or giving free rein to their thoughts, yet exercising control,
they can serve as models for the world.
Eating according to the measure of their appetite,
clothing according to their physique,
dwelling in spaces that accommodate their bodies,
acting in ways that suit their dispositions—
leaving the surplus of the world without possessing it,
entrusting all things to it without seeking profit—
how could they lose their inherent nature and destiny due to poverty, wealth, honor, or lowliness!
Those who are like this
may be said to truly embody the Dào.
3.5. Guarding Purity Five
Lǎozi said:
Humans receive their vital breath from Heaven;
the ears and eyes regarding sounds and sights,
the nose and mouth regarding scents and odors,
the skin regarding cold and warmth—
their inherent responses are the same.
Yet some die because of them,
some live because of them,
some become noble persons,
some become petty persons—
the difference lies in what controls them.
The spirit is the deep pool of wisdom;
when the spirit is clear, wisdom is bright.
Wisdom is the storehouse of the heart;
when wisdom is impartial, the heart is calm.
People do not mirror themselves in flowing muddy water but in still clear water,
because it is clear and calm.
Thus, only when the spirit is clear and the mind calm can one reflect the true nature of things.
Therefore, those who use this must rely on what is not used.
A mirror that is bright is not soiled by dust and grime;
a spirit that is clear is not led astray by desires.
Thus, when the heart focuses on something,
the spirit intently attends to it;
returning it to emptiness,
then agitation dissipates and rest is preserved—
this is the roaming of the sage.
Therefore, those in ancient times who governed the world
necessarily understood the true condition of inherent nature and destiny before they could do so.
3.6. Guarding Authenticity Six
Lǎozi said:
Those called sages
simply suit their true disposition;
they eat according to the measure of their appetite,
clothe according to their physique,
and regulate themselves—that is all.
Thus, greedy and corrupt thoughts have no way to arise.
Therefore, those who can possess the world
necessarily do not act for the sake of the world;
those who can have fame and reputation
necessarily do not seek them through hasty action.
Genuinely understanding the true condition of inherent nature and destiny,
benevolence and righteousness then adhere naturally.
As for when the spirit has nothing obscuring it,
the heart has nothing burdening it,
when one is thoroughly penetrating and unobstructed,
serenely free of affairs,
then power and profit cannot seduce,
sounds and sights cannot debauch,
sophists cannot persuade,
the clever cannot stir,
the brave cannot intimidate—
this is the roaming of the authentic person.
That which gives life to life does not itself live;
that which transforms transformation does not itself transform.
Those who do not understand this Dào,
even if their wisdom encompasses Heaven and Earth,
their brightness illuminates like the sun and moon,
their arguments unravel interlocked rings,
their words polish metal and stone,
still are of no benefit in governing the world.
Therefore, the sage does not lose what he guards.
3.7. Guarding Stillness Seven
Lǎozi said:
Quietude, solitude, calmness, and simplicity
are the means to nurture life;
harmony, joy, emptiness, and non-being
are the means to uphold virtue.
When the outer does not disturb the inner, then nature attains its proper state;
when stillness does not stir harmony, then virtue rests securely in its place.
Nurturing life to traverse the world,
embracing virtue to complete one's years—
this may be called truly embodying the Dào.
If one is like this,
the blood vessels have no stagnation,
the five viscera have no accumulated energy,
fortune and calamity cannot cause deviation,
blame and praise cannot gather as dust.
Without the appropriate era,
who can succeed?
Having the talent,
but not encountering the right time,
one still cannot extricate oneself—
how much more so without the Dào!
Those whose eyes examine the tip of an autumn hair
do not hear the sound of thunderclaps with their ears;
those whose ears are attuned to the sounds of metal and jade
do not see the form of Mount Tài with their eyes.
Thus, when one focuses on small things,
then great things are forgotten.
Now the coming of the myriad things
plucks and uproots our nature,
seizes and takes our essence,
like a fountainhead—
even if we wish not to receive it,
how could it be possible?
Now, if a basin of water is left clear for a full day,
then it reflects eyebrows and lashes;
cloud it with just one stir,
and it cannot reflect squares and circles.
Human spirit and vitality are difficult to clear and easy to cloud—
just like the basin of water.
3.8. Guarding the Law Eight
Lǎozi said: The highest sages emulate Heaven,
the next best honor the worthy,
the inferior appoint ministers.
Appointing ministers is the path to peril and ruin;
honoring the worthy is the source of confusion and delusion;
emulating Heaven is the way to govern Heaven and Earth.
Emptiness and stillness are paramount;
emptiness and non-being receive everything,
stillness and non-action hold everything.
Knowing the Dào of emptiness and stillness,
one can then persist from beginning to end.
Therefore, the sage takes stillness as order
and movement as disorder.
Hence it is said: Do not disturb, do not interfere,
and the myriad things will clear themselves;
do not startle, do not frighten,
and the myriad things will order themselves—
this is called the Dào of Heaven.
3.9. Guarding Weakness Nine
Lǎozi said:
The Son of Heaven, dukes, and marquises regard the world or a state as their family,
and the myriad things as their possessions.
Embracing the vastness of the world,
possessing the multitude of the myriad things,
their vital energy becomes inflated and their will arrogant.
The great ones use military force to invade the small,
the small ones act arrogantly to bully their superiors.
Their minds are extravagant and broad—
like a gale wind and torrential rain,
they cannot last long.
Therefore, the sage restrains them with the Dào,
holding to Oneness and non-action
without harming the harmonious energy.
Seeing the small and guarding the soft,
retreating and not possessing,
they take the rivers and seas as their model.
The rivers and seas do not act,
thus achievement and fame transform naturally;
they do not force,
thus they can become kings.
Being the feminine of the world,
thus their spirit does not die;
loving themselves,
thus they can achieve their nobility.
With the power of ten thousand chariots,
one takes all things as achievements and fame,
authority and responsibility are extremely heavy,
one must not belittle oneself,
for self-belittlement prevents the accomplishment of achievements and fame.
The Way,
the great is accomplished through the small,
the multitude is governed by the few,
thus the sage rules the world with the Way,
gentleness and subtlety manifest smallness,
frugality and restraint manifest fewness,
by manifesting smallness, one can thus accomplish greatness,
by manifesting fewness, one can thus achieve beauty.
The Way of Heaven,
suppresses the high and lifts the low,
reduces the excessive,
and supplements the insufficient,
rivers and seas occupy the lowly places of the earth,
thus all under heaven return to and serve them.
Therefore, the sage is humble and modest,
clarity, tranquility, deference, and yielding manifest lowness,
an open mind and emptiness manifest insufficiency,
by manifesting lowness, one can thus attain height,
by manifesting insufficiency, one can thus achieve worthiness.
The arrogant cannot stand,
the extravagant cannot last,
the violent will die,
the overflowing will perish,
fierce winds and torrential rains do not last all day,
small valleys cannot remain full for even a moment;
fierce winds and sudden rains act with violent energy,
thus they cannot last long and vanish,
small valleys occupy forceful positions,
thus they cannot avoid being depleted.
Therefore, the sage holds to the feminine,
abandons pride and extravagance,
dare not act with violent energy,
by holding to the feminine,
one can thus establish masculinity,
by avoiding pride and extravagance,
one can thus endure long.
Lǎozǐ said:
The Way of Heaven reaches its extreme and then reverses,
fullness leads to diminishment,
as seen with the sun and moon.
Thus the sage daily diminishes and maintains a humble spirit without self-satisfaction,
daily advances with femininity,
so that merit and virtue do not decline,
for such is the Way of Heaven.
Human nature tends to favor height and despise lowness,
to favor gain and despise loss,
to favor benefit and despise harm,
to favor honor and despise lowliness,
to favor nobility and despise baseness,
when the multitude pursues these,
they cannot achieve,
when they grasp them,
they cannot obtain.
Therefore, the sage emulates Heaven,
accomplishes without acting,
obtains without grasping,
shares common feelings with others but follows a different path,
thus able to endure long.
Thus the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors had a warning vessel,
named the Yòuzhī,
when empty it stands upright,
when full it topples over.
For things flourish and then decay,
the sun reaches its zenith and then declines,
the moon becomes full and then wanes,
joy ends and sorrow follows,
therefore, broad intelligence and vast wisdom are guarded by simplicity,
extensive learning and eloquence are guarded by restraint,
martial prowess and courage are guarded by caution,
wealth and high status are guarded by modesty,
benevolence bestowed upon the world is guarded by humility,
these five are how the ancient kings guarded the world.
"Those who follow this Way do not desire fullness,
thus they can remain worn yet not newly completed."
Lǎozǐ said:
The sage closes with the yīn,
opens with the yáng,
able to reach a state of no joy,
then there is nothing not joyful,
nothing not joyful is the ultimate joy.
Thus, inner joy affects the outer,
not outer joy affecting the inner,
therefore, there is self-joy,
which leads to attainment,
valued throughout the world.
The reason for this is,
acting for the world through the world.
The essence of the world,
lies not in others but in oneself,
not in others but in one's own person,
when the person attains it, all things are complete.
Therefore, those who understand the discourse on mental cultivation,
place desires, preferences, and aversions outside.
Thus, there is nothing to delight in,
nothing to anger,
nothing to enjoy,
nothing to suffer,
all things mysteriously unite,
without right or wrong.
Thus, scholars have steadfast principles,
women have unchanging conduct,
revered without relying on power,
wealthy without needing riches,
strong without requiring force,
not profiting from goods and wealth,
not coveting worldly fame,
not considering high status as security,
not considering low status as danger,
form, spirit, energy, and will each reside in their proper place.
The form is the dwelling of life,
energy is the origin of life,
spirit is the controller of life,
if one loses its position, the other two are harmed,
thus when spirit is the master, the form follows and benefits,
when the form is the master, the spirit follows and is harmed.
Greedy and desire-ridden individuals,
are deluded by power and profit,
enticed by fame and position,
nearly surpassing others in knowledge,
holding high positions in the world,
their spirit daily depletes and drifts away,
long immersed without return,
the form closed and inwardly resistant,
thus there is no way to enter,
hence often suffering from blindness, forgetfulness, and self-loss.
Spirit, essence, will, and energy,
when calm, daily replenish and strengthen,
when agitated, daily deplete and age;
therefore, the sage nurtures their spirit,
softens their energy,
calms their form,
and floats and sinks with the Way;
thus, the transformations of all things all find their match,
the changes of all affairs all find their response.
3.10. Guarding Simplicity
Lǎozǐ said:
The so-called Zhēnrén,
have a nature in harmony with the Way.
Thus, having yet as if without,
substantial yet as if empty,
cultivating the inner, not the outer,
clear and plain, supremely simple,
acting without action and returning to simplicity.
Embracing the root and holding the spirit,
they wander at the root of heaven and earth,
vaguely roaming beyond the dust and grime,
carefree in the work of non-action.
Mechanical wisdom and cunning,
are not carried in the heart,
examining the unadorned,
not shifting with things,
observing the transformations of affairs,
yet guarding their origin.
Mind and intent focused within,
understanding fortune and misfortune as one,
dwelling without knowing what they do,
moving without knowing where they go.
Knowing without learning,
seeing without looking,
accomplishing without acting,
discerning without governing,
responding when stimulated,
moving when pressed,
going when compelled,
like the radiance of light,
like the following of a shadow,
taking the Way as their guide,
acting when conditions arise,
expansively empty,
clear, calm, and without thought,
regarding a thousand lives as one transformation,
myriad differences as one origin.
Having essence but not using it,
having spirit but not employing it,
guarding the simplicity of great chaos,
standing within the utmost essence,
sleeping without dreams,
wisdom without sprouting,
moving without form,
still without substance,
existing as if gone,
living as if dead,
passing through without gaps,
commanding spirits and ghosts,
this is how the spirit can ascend and reach the Way.
Enabling the spirit to flow freely without losing its origin,
day and night without gaps, harmonizing with things in springlike vitality,
this is uniting and generating timeliness within the heart.
Thus the form may decay but the spirit never transforms,
responding to change with non-transformation,
undergoing countless changes and turns without beginning or end.
What transforms returns to formlessness,
while what does not transform is born together with heaven and earth.
Therefore, that which gives life has never lived,
yet what it gives life to lives;
that which transforms has never transformed,
yet what it transforms does transform.
This is the wandering of the true person,
the way of purity and simplicity.
Lǎozǐ said:
The Dào is supremely high with nothing above it,
immeasurably deep with nothing below it,
level as a water-level,
straight as a marking-line,
round as a compass,
square as a T-square,
enveloping heaven and earth without inside or outside,
penetrating and covering all without obstruction.
Therefore, those who embody the Dào
are neither angry nor joyful,
sit without worry,
sleep without dreaming,
name things when they see them,
and respond when events occur.
Lǎozǐ said:
Those who desire to be masters of reputation must do good,
those who desire to do good must create affairs,
creating affairs means abandoning the public for the private,
turning away from the Dào to follow oneself.
Wishing to be praised for doing good,
establishing names to become worthy,
means governance does not follow principle and affairs do not accord with timing.
Governance not following principle brings much blame,
affairs not according with timing bring no achievement.
Reckless action to seek advantage,
even if successful, cannot cover the blame,
and if affairs fail, it is enough to destroy oneself.
Lǎozǐ said:
Do not be the master of reputation,
do not be the storehouse of schemes,
do not be the undertaker of affairs,
do not be the proprietor of wisdom.
Hide in formlessness,
act without haste,
do not precede blessings,
do not initiate misfortune;
begin in formlessness,
move only when compelled.
To desire blessings, first have no misfortune;
to desire gain, first stay far from harm.
Thus, those who are tranquil through non-action:
losing that by which they are tranquil means danger;
those who govern through non-action:
losing that by which they govern means chaos.
Therefore,
"Do not wish to be prized like jade,
nor despised like stone."
The animal with beautiful fur will be skinned,
the one with fine horns will be killed,
sweet springs will surely run dry,
straight trees will surely be felled.
Flowery words later bring fault;
if a mountain contains jade,
the mountain is damaged.
The common people's trouble
indeed lies before words.
Lǎozǐ said:
In moving with the times,
follow along accordingly.
Those who don't know the Dào turn blessings into misfortune.
Heaven as the canopy,
earth as the carriage box,
those skilled in using the Dào never exhaust it;
earth as the carriage box,
heaven as the canopy,
those skilled in using the Dào never come to harm.
Array the five phases and one will surely overcome another;
what heaven covers is all appropriately matched.
Therefore,
"To know when one does not know is best,
not to know when one knows is a defect."
Lǎozǐ said:
Mountains produce metal,
stones produce jade,
yet they are反过来 stripped;
trees produce insects,
which then eat them;
humans create affairs,
which then harm them.
Those who delight in affairs never avoid being struck,
those who contend for profit never avoid exhaustion;
good swimmers drown,
good riders fall,
each because of what they are good at
turns it into their own misfortune.
Gain lies in timing,
not in contention;
order lies in the Dào,
not in sagehood.
Earth stays low,
not contending for height,
thus secure without danger;
water flows downward,
not contending for speed,
thus moves away without delay.
"Therefore the sage, because he does not contend, is without loss;
because he does not act, is without failure."
Lǎozǐ said:
With one saying, one cannot be exhausted,
with two sayings, the world follows,
with three sayings, one leads the feudal lords,
with four sayings, one matches the world.
With integrity and trustworthiness, one cannot be exhausted,
with the Dào and virtue, the world follows,
promoting the worthy and virtuous,
one leads the feudal lords,
hating few and loving many, one matches the world.
Lǎozǐ said:
Humans have three deaths
not due to destiny:
eating and drinking without moderation,
neglecting and debasing their bodies,
sickness kills them;
insatiable desire for pleasure,
unceasing pursuit of gain,
punishment kills them;
opposing the many with few,
challenging the strong while weak,
weapons kill them.
Lǎozǐ said:
Those who give generously receive beautiful回报,
those who create great enmity suffer deep misfortune.
To give little but expect much,
to store up resentment yet suffer no harm -
this has never happened.
Examine how one treats others,
and you will know what comes back to you.
Lǎozǐ said:
Understand heavenly mandate,
cultivate mental discipline,
regulate likes and dislikes,
harmonize emotions and nature,
then the way of governance is clear.
Understanding heavenly mandate means not being confused about fortune and misfortune,
cultivating mental discipline means not indulging in arbitrary joy or anger,
regulating likes and dislikes means not coveting the useless,
harmonizing emotions and nature means desires do not exceed limits.
Not being confused about fortune and misfortune means movement and stillness follow principle,
not indulging in arbitrary joy or anger means rewards and punishments are impartial,
not coveting the useless means not harming nature with desires,
desires not exceeding limits means nurturing life and knowing contentment.
All these four things
are not sought from without,
not borrowed from others,
but obtained by turning within.
Lǎozǐ said:
Do not seek blameworthy conduct,
do not resent others for blaming you;
cultivate virtue worthy of praise,
but do not seek others' praise.
You cannot prevent misfortune from coming,
but trust yourself not to invite it;
you cannot ensure blessings arrive,
but trust yourself not to refuse them.
When misfortune comes, it is not born from you,
so when in difficulty, do not worry;
when blessings come, they are not achieved by you,
so when successful, do not boast.
Therefore, be content in quiet living,
and govern through non-action.
Lǎozi said:
The Dào maintains what one already possesses,
and does not seek what one has not yet obtained.
Seeking what is not yet obtained leads to the loss of what one has,
while following what one already has brings the arrival of what is desired.
Governing what is not yet solid leads to disorder,
and those who actively strive for order will certainly face danger.
Actions are not entirely free from fault,
yet those who urgently seek fame will inevitably be thwarted.
Thus, there is no greater blessing than being free from calamity,
and no greater gain than avoiding loss.
"Therefore, for all things, sometimes adding to them leads to diminishment,
and diminishing them leads to increase."
The Dào cannot encourage the pursuit of profit,
but it can pacify the spirit and avert harm.
Thus, it often brings absence of calamity rather than constant good fortune,
and often brings absence of blame rather than constant achievement.
The Dào is described as vast and obscure,
following the majesty of Heaven,
sharing the same qì as Heaven,
without deliberate thought,
without contrived preparations,
not welcoming what comes,
