not escorting what departs.
Though people may go east, west, south, or north,
it stands alone at the center.
Thus, even amidst widespread distortion,
it does not lose its uprightness;
flowing along with all under heaven,
it does not leave its domain.
It does not pursue beauty,
nor avoid ugliness,
but follows the way of Heaven.
It does not initiate,
nor insist on its own ways,
but follows the principles of Heaven.
It does not plan in advance,
nor neglect the timing,
but aligns with Heaven's schedule.
It does not seek gains,
nor refuse blessings,
but follows the rules of Heaven.
Internally, there is no extraordinary fortune,
externally, no extraordinary disaster,
thus calamity and blessing do not arise,
and how could there be harm from others?
Therefore, the highest virtue shares the same strategy in speech,
the same purpose in action,
with superiors and inferiors of one mind,
without divergent paths or sidelong views.
Rejecting what is wicked,
and opening the way to goodness,
the people then turn toward righteousness.
Lǎozi said:
Doing good brings encouragement,
doing ill brings scrutiny,
encouragement leads to honor,
scrutiny leads to trouble.
Thus, the Dào cannot be used to advance and seek fame,
but can be used to retreat and cultivate oneself.
Therefore, the sage does not seek fame through action,
nor praise through knowledge,
governing in accordance with spontaneity,
with no personal involvement.
Those who act may not succeed,
those who seek may not obtain,
humans have limitations but the Dào is all-penetrating.
Having wisdom yet non-action achieves the same result as having no wisdom,
having ability yet non-striving achieves the same virtue as having no ability.
Having wisdom as if without wisdom,
having ability as if without ability,
then the principles of Dào are comprehended and human talents fade.
Human and Dào cannot both be prominent,
if humans love fame, they do not use the Dào,
if the Dào prevails over humans, fame ceases,
when the Dào ceases and fame becomes prominent, danger and destruction follow.
Lǎozi said:
Having trustworthy men distribute wealth
is不如 as drawing lots with fixed shares,
why so?
Because those with intentions towards fairness
are不如 as those without intentions.
Having honest men guard wealth
is不如 as locking the door and sealing it completely,
for those with desires towards honesty
are不如 as those without desires.
When people are pointed out their flaws, they resent it,
yet a mirror that shows one's ugliness is considered a good mirror.
If one can interact with things without involving oneself,
then one is free from burdens.
Lǎozi said:
In serving others,
if not with precious gifts,
then必定 with humble words.
But when gifts are exhausted, desires are not satisfied,
and humble postures and flattering words,
with persuasive speeches, fail to establish bonds,
and oaths and alliances made,
once agreed upon are broken soon after,
therefore the noble person does not outwardly adorn with benevolence and righteousness,
but inwardly cultivates the Dào and virtue.
Attending to affairs within his borders,
making the most of his land's expanse,
encouraging the people to hold fast even unto death,
strengthening his city walls,
uniting superiors and inferiors as one,
guarding the altars of soil and grain together,
then those seeking fame will not attack the innocent,
those seeking profit will not assault the hard-to-obtain.
This is the way to preserve wholeness,
the principle that ensures benefit.
Lǎozi said:
The sage overcomes his heart-mind,
the multitude overcomes their desires.
The noble person acts with upright qì,
the petty person acts with wicked qì.
What is inwardly harmonious with one's nature,
outwardly conforms to righteousness,
acting according to principle,
unbound by external things—
this is upright qì.
Indulging in flavors,
excess in sounds and sights,
acting out of joy and anger,
without regard for future troubles—
this is wicked qì.
Wicked and upright injure each other,
desires and nature harm one another,
they cannot coexist,
one rises as the other falls.
Therefore, the sage reduces desires to follow nature.
The eyes delight in colors,
the ears in sounds,
the nose in fragrances,
the mouth in flavors—
united they bring pleasure,
inseparable from benefit and harm—
this is desire.
If the eyes, ears, nose, and mouth do not know what to take or reject,
the heart-mind should regulate them,
so each attains its proper place.
From this perspective,
it is clear that desires cannot be completely overcome.
Lǎozi said:
In governing the body and nurturing nature,
moderate rest and activity,
balance eating and drinking,
harmonize joy and anger,
facilitate movement and stillness.
When what is within oneself is attained,
wicked qì has no way to enter.
Adorning the exterior injures the interior,
indulging emotions harms the spirit,
focusing on appearances obscures the truth.
Those who never forget their worthiness even for a moment
will certainly burden their nature.
Those who never forget their appearance even within a hundred steps
will certainly encumber their form.
Thus, beautiful wings harm the bones,
lush branches and leaves harm the roots.
To have both beauties is impossible under heaven.
Lǎozi said:
Heaven has light but does not worry about the people's darkness,
Earth has wealth but does not worry about the people's poverty.
Those who have attained the Dào are like hills and mountains,
solid and unmoving,
providing a reference for travelers,
upright in themselves and sufficient for things,
not bestowing gifts upon people,
and those who use them do not receive their virtue,
thus they remain secure and enduring.
Heaven and Earth give nothing,
so nothing is taken from them;
they confer no virtue,
so they incur no resentment.
Those prone to anger必然 accumulate much resentment,
those generous in giving必然 are skilled in taking away.
Only by following the spontaneity of Heaven and Earth can one master principle.
Thus, where praise appears, slander follows;
where good appears, evil accompanies;
profit is the beginning of harm,
fortune is the precursor to calamity.
Not seeking profit means having no calamity.
The body takes wholeness as its constant state,
wealth and honor are but temporary lodgings.
Lǎozi said:
The sage has no extravagant clothing,
no bizarre conduct.
His attire is not mixed,
his actions are not for show.
When successful, he is not ostentatious;
when in hardship, he is not intimidated.
When honored, he does not flaunt;
when in seclusion, he suffers no disgrace.
Though different, he is not considered strange;
though sharing common functions, he cannot be named.
This is called great penetration.
Lǎozi said:
The Dào is about rectifying oneself and awaiting destiny.
When the time comes, one cannot welcome it and then turn it back;
when the time departs, one cannot pursue it and pull it back.
Thus, the sage does not advance to seek,
nor retreat to yield.
If one follows the times for three years,
the time may leave and I run after it;
if one avoids the times for three years,
the time may be behind me.
Neither leaving nor approaching,
he stands firm in his own place.
The way of heaven has no favorites;
it is only with virtue that it sides.
When blessings arrive, it is not because one sought them;
thus, he does not boast of his merits.
When calamities come, it is not because he generated them;
thus, he does not regret his actions.
His heart is tranquil,
not encumbered by virtue.
The barking of dogs does not startle him;
he trusts in his own nature.
Sincerely, he has no improper desires;
thus, one who comprehends the Dào is not confused,
and one who knows destiny does not worry.
When an emperor or king passes away,
his bones are buried in the wild,
yet he is sacrificed to in the bright hall—
this shows that the spirit is more valued than the form.
Thus, when the spirit governs the form, it follows;
when the form overcomes the spirit, it leads to exhaustion.
Though intelligence and hearing are used,
they must return to the spirit—
this is called great penetration.
Lǎozi said:
Those in ancient times who preserved themselves
delighted in virtue and forgot their lowliness;
thus, fame did not sway their will.
They delighted in the Dào and forgot their poverty;
thus, profit did not move their hearts.
Therefore, they could be humble and yet joyful,
calm and yet serene.
To worry about the chaos under heaven
with the limited span of life,
is like worrying about the river drying up
and shedding tears to add to it.
Thus, one who does not worry about the chaos under heaven,
but delights in governing his own person,
can be spoken to about the Dào.
Lǎozi said:
There are three sources of resentment among people:
those with high rank are envied by others,
those with great office are disliked by their rulers,
those with ample emoluments are resented by others.
Thus, the higher the rank, the more humble one's intentions should be;
the greater the office, the more cautious one's heart should be;
the more ample the emoluments, the broader one's generosity should be.
Cultivating these three, resentment does not arise.
"Therefore, the noble takes the humble as its root,
the high takes the low as its foundation."
Lǎozi said:
Speech is the means to communicate oneself to others;
hearing is the means to understand others for oneself.
If one is both blind and deaf,
the way of human communication is blocked.
Thus, those who suffer from blindness and deafness
do not know how to manage communication.
But is it only the physical body that can be blind and deaf?
The heart can be so too.
When the heart is blocked,
one does not know the means of communication—
this is the category of blindness and deafness.
Now, the Dào as the fundamental source
gives birth to all that has form;
as a parent, it is also intimate.
Those who enjoy grains and breathe energy all attain longevity;
as a ruler, it is also benevolent.
All the wise learn from it;
as a teacher, it is also illuminating.
People often harm the useful with the useless,
thus knowledge is not broadened and the days seem insufficient.
If one uses the time spent on games to inquire about the Dào,
one's hearing and insight will deepen.
Not hearing and not inquiring
is like being blind and deaf compared to others.
Lǎozi said:
Human nature is such that the heart submits to virtue,
not to force.
Virtue lies in giving,
not in seeking.
Thus, if the sage desires to be valued by others,
he first values others;
if he desires to be respected by others,
he first respects others;
if he desires to surpass others,
he first surpasses himself;
if he desires to humble others,
he first humbles himself.
Therefore, nobility and humility, respect and lowliness
are governed by the Dào.
The ancient sage kings humbled themselves through their words,
placed themselves behind others—
thus, all under heaven gladly supported them without weariness,
upheld them without finding them burdensome.
This is because their virtue was abundant and their energy harmonious.
Thus, to know that giving is taking,
that being behind is being ahead—
this is close to the Dào.
Lǎozi said:
One with little virtue but much favor is criticized;
one with low ability but high position is in danger;
one with no great merit but ample emoluments is in peril.
Therefore,
"Some things may be benefited and yet harmed,
or harmed and yet benefited."
The multitude only knows to profit from profit,
but does not know to treat illness as illness.
Only the sage knows that illness can be profit,
and profit can be illness.
Thus, a tree that bears fruit twice will have its roots injured;
a family that hoards much will inevitably have disaster for its descendants.
Great profit, in turn, becomes harm—
such is the way of heaven.
Lǎozi said:
The petty person in action seeks random gain,
the noble person seeks random righteousness.
One who does good
does not seek fame,
yet fame follows him.
Fame does not make an appointment with profit,
yet profit returns to him.
What they seek is the same,
but what they expect is different.
Thus, when an action brings benefit,
loss follows it.
One whose words are never constant,
whose actions are never appropriate,
is a petty person.
One who examines one matter,
is proficient in one skill,
is an average person.
One who covers all and possesses both,
who masters skills and employs talents,
is a sage.
Lǎozi said:
Life is what we borrow,
death is where we return.
Thus, in times of order, use righteousness to guard the body;
in times of chaos, use the body to guard righteousness.
The day of death
is the end of one's actions.
Thus, the noble person is cautious and uses it only once.
Life is received from heaven,
destiny is encountered through the times.
To have talent but not meet the right era
is heaven's doing.
Seek it by the Dào,
but obtaining it lies in destiny.
Thus, the noble person can do good but cannot necessarily attain fortune;
he cannot bear to do wrong,
but cannot necessarily avoid calamity.
Therefore, the noble person advances when the time is right,
gaining it through righteousness—
what fortune is there in that!
He retreats when the time is not right,
yielding with propriety—
what misfortune is there in that!
Thus, even in poverty and lowliness, if he does not regret,
it is because he has obtained what he values.
Lǎozǐ said:
Humans possess harmonious and contrary energies born from the heart.
When the heart is ordered, energy flows harmoniously;
when the heart is disordered, energy becomes contrary.
The order or disorder of the heart lies in the Dào.
Attaining the Dào brings order to the heart;
losing the Dào brings disorder to the heart.
An ordered heart leads to mutual deference;
a disordered heart leads to mutual contention.
Deference yields virtue;
contention breeds harm.
Virtue allows energy to flow harmoniously;
harm causes energy to turn contrary.
Harmonious energy leads to self-sacrifice for others;
contrary energy leads to harming others for self-gain.
This energy can be mastered through the Dào.
The way of Heaven
is like an echo responding to a sound.
Accumulating virtue brings fortune;
accumulating misfortune brings resentment.
Learning falters amid abundant official duties;
filial piety declines with wife and children;
calamity arises from resolved worries;
illness worsens just as it seems to heal.
Therefore,
"If one remains as cautious at the end as at the beginning,
there will be no failed affairs."
Lǎozǐ said:
Associating with the crooked and the straight,
how can one not gain?
But associating with the straight and the crooked,
do not follow them blindly.
This is what is meant by being in the same mud but different in filth.
Lǎozǐ said:
Sages equate life and death;
fools also equate life and death.
Sages equate them with clarity of principle;
fools equate them without knowing where benefit and harm lie.
The Dào hangs in heaven;
things are spread upon the earth;
harmony resides in humans.
If the ruler lacks harmony, heavenly energy does not descend,
earthly energy does not rise,
yīn and yáng fall out of balance,
wind and rain come untimely,
and the people suffer illness and hunger.
Lǎozǐ said:
Gaining the arms of ten thousand soldiers
is not as good as hearing one fitting word.
Obtaining the pearl of the Marquis of Suí
is not as good as understanding the origin of affairs.
Acquiring the jade of Héshì
is not as good as knowing what suits the situation.
Though the world be vast,
those fond of using arms perish;
though the state be secure,
those who love war endanger it.
Hence,
"In a small state with few people,
even if there are tools ten or a hundred times more efficient, they are not used."
Lǎozǐ said:
Those who can achieve hegemony
must be ones whose virtue prevails.
Those who can overcome enemies
must be strong.
Those who can be strong
must employ human effort.
Those who can employ human effort
must have won people's hearts.
Those who can win people's hearts
must have attained self-mastery.
Those who can attain self-mastery
must be gentle and weak.
Strength overcomes those inferior to oneself,
but meets its match against equals.
Gentleness overcomes those superior to oneself,
its power immeasurable.
Thus, to turn many defeats into great victory—
only a sage can do this.
Wénzǐ inquired about the Dào.
Lǎozǐ said:
If learning is not refined,
one hears the Dào but not deeply.
Generally, listening
serves to attain wisdom,
to accomplish conduct,
and to achieve merit and fame.
Without refinement, there is no clarity;
without depth, there is no penetration.
Thus, superior learning listens with the spirit;
middling learning listens with the heart;
inferior learning listens with the ears.
Those who listen with ears
learn only on the skin;
those who listen with the heart
learn in the muscles;
those who listen with the spirit
learn in the marrow.
Hence, if listening is not deep,
understanding is not clear;
if understanding is not clear,
one cannot exhaust its essence;
if one cannot exhaust its essence,
practice will not succeed.
The principle of listening:
empty the heart, be pure and still,
reduce energy, avoid excess,
have no thoughts, no worries,
let eyes not gaze recklessly,
ears not listen carelessly.
Focus essence, accumulate and store,
inner intent full and concentrated.
Once attained,
hold it firmly,
make it long-lasting.
Now the Dào,
originating, has a beginning,
starting from softness and weakness,
maturing into firmness and strength;
beginning with scarcity and fewness,
growing into abundance and multitude.
A tree ten arm-spans around
starts from a handful;
a tower a hundred ren high
begins from below.
This is the way of Heaven.
Sages emulate it:
humility is how one places oneself below;
retreat is how one stays behind;
frugality is how one makes oneself small;
reduction is how one makes oneself less.
Through humility comes honor;
through retreat comes precedence;
through frugality comes breadth;
through reduction comes greatness.
This is how the heavenly Dào accomplishes things.
Now the Dào
is the source of virtue,
the root of heaven,
the gate of blessings.
All things depend on it to be born,
depend on it to be completed,
depend on it to be at peace.
The Dào
is non-active and formless,
inwardly used to cultivate the self,
outwardly used to govern others.
When achievements are made and affairs established,
it neighbors with heaven.
Non-active, yet nothing is left undone;
none know its emotion,
none know its truth,
yet within it is faithfulness.
If the Son of Heaven has the Dào, the world submits;
he long preserves the altars of land and grain.
If lords and marquises have the Dào, the people are harmonious;
they do not lose their states.
If officers and commoners have the Dào, they preserve their persons;
they protect their kin.
If the strong and great have the Dào,
they conquer without battle;
if the small and weak have the Dào,
they gain without contention.
If undertakings are based on the Dào,
success brings fortune.
If ruler and minister have the Dào, there is loyalty and kindness;
if father and son have the Dào, there is affection and filial piety;
if officers and commoners have the Dào, they love one another.
Thus, with the Dào there is harmony;
without the Dào there is harshness.
From this we see,
for humans, the Dào
is appropriate in all things.
As for the Way,
practicing it on a small scale brings small blessings,
practicing it on a large scale brings great blessings,
practicing it fully makes the world submit,
submission leads to heartfelt allegiance.
Thus, the Dì is
one whom the world deems appropriate;
the Wáng is
one toward whom the world inclines.
If the world finds neither appropriate nor inclined,
they cannot be called Dì or Wáng.
Hence, without gaining people, the Dìwáng cannot achieve success;
gaining people but losing the Way, they cannot maintain it either.
Those who lose the Way
are extravagant, arrogant, and indulgent,
haughty and self-conceited,
seeing surplus, they flaunt and boast,
holding to dominance and stubbornness,
they stir trouble and incur resentment,
becoming leaders of conflict,
instigators of chaos.
If petty people practice this,
they suffer great personal calamity;
if great people practice this,
the state perishes,
shallowly affecting themselves,
deeply affecting their descendants.
Thus, no crime is greater than being without the Way,
no resentment deeper than being without virtue,
for such is the Way of Heaven.
Lǎozǐ said:
Those who practice the Way
make it so that even if others are brave,
they cannot pierce them;
even if skilled,
they cannot strike them.
Yet, being unpierced
and unstruck
still brings humiliation;
it is not as good as making the brave dare not pierce,
the skilled dare not strike.
But daring not
does not mean lacking the intent;
it is not as good as making them have no such intent.
Having no intent
means lacking a heart of love and benefit;
it is not as good as making all men and women under heaven
joyfully desire to love and benefit them.
If so,
even without land, one can be a ruler;
without office, one can be a leader;
all under heaven will wish to secure and benefit them.
Wénzǐ asked about virtue.
Lǎozi said:
Nurturing and rearing them,
helping them thrive and grow,
benefiting all without discrimination,
harmonizing with heaven and earth—
this is called virtue.
What is benevolence?
Answer: As a superior, not boasting of one's merits;
as a subordinate, not ashamed of one's flaws;
in great matters, not arrogant;
in small matters, not negligent;
loving all without selfishness,
enduring without decline—
this is called benevolence.
What is righteousness?
Answer: As a superior, aiding the weak;
as a subordinate, upholding integrity;
in success, not acting wantonly;
in hardship, not changing principles;
adhering to standards and following reason,
not twisting for private gain—
this is called righteousness.
What is propriety?
Answer: As a superior, being respectful and stern;
as a subordinate, being humble and reverent;
yielding and maintaining gentleness,
being the receptive under heaven;
standing in not daring,
setting in not being able—
this is called propriety.
Thus, cultivating virtue makes subordinates obey commands;
cultivating benevolence makes subordinates not contend;
cultivating righteousness makes subordinates fair and upright;
cultivating propriety makes subordinates respectful;
when these four are cultivated,
the state is peaceful and stable.
Hence, the birth of things comes from the Way,
growth from virtue,
affection from benevolence,
correctness from righteousness,
reverence from propriety.
Without nurturing and rearing,
they cannot thrive and grow;
without kindness and love,
they cannot achieve completion;
without correctness and guidance,
they cannot endure long;
without respect and honor,
they cannot be valued.
Thus, virtue is what the people value;
benevolence is what the people cherish;
righteousness is what the people fear;
propriety is what the people revere.
These four
are the order of culture,
by which the sage governs all things.
If the noble person lacks virtue, subordinates resent;
lacks benevolence, subordinates contend;
lacks righteousness, subordinates become violent;
lacks propriety, subordinates fall into chaos.
If these four constants are not established,
it is called being without the Way.
That which is without the Way does not perish
has never been.
Lǎozi said:
In the age of perfect virtue,
merchants traded conveniently in markets,
farmers enjoyed their work in fields, [125 officials were content in their duties,
scholars cultivated their path,
the people delighted in their livelihoods;
thus, wind and rain did not destroy,
plants and trees did not die young,
the river produced charts,
the Luò produced writings.
When the age declined,
taxes were levied without limit,
killings knew no end,
advisers were punished,
worthy scholars executed,
thus mountains crumbled, rivers dried,
creatures stirred incessantly,
fields bore no vegetables.
Hence, in a well-governed age, the foolish cannot alone cause chaos;
in a chaotic age, the worthy cannot alone bring order.
Therefore, the sage is harmonious, serene, and tranquil—
this is their nature;
achieving aspirations and practicing the Way—
this is their destiny.
Thus, life encounters destiny to then act,
destiny meets the time to then become clear;
there must be the right age before there can be the right person.
Wénzǐ asked about sagehood and wisdom.
Lǎozi said:
To know by hearing—
that is sagehood;
to know by seeing—
that is wisdom.
Thus, the sage often hears the origins of fortune and misfortune and chooses the path;
the wise often see the forms of fortune and misfortune and choose their actions.
The sage knows the auspicious and inauspicious ways of Heaven,
thus knowing the origins of fortune and misfortune;
the wise foresee the forms,
thus knowing the gateways to fortune and misfortune.
Hearing the unformed is sagehood;
foreseeing the formed is wisdom;
those without hearing or sight
are foolish and deluded.
Lǎozi said:
If a ruler favors cleverness,
they oppose the times and rely on themselves,
abandoning natural patterns to use scheming.
With vast things and shallow wisdom,
using the shallow to cover the vast—
none have ever succeeded.
Relying solely on one's wisdom,
losses are bound to be many.
Favoring cleverness
is a path to exhaustion;
favoring bravery
is a way to peril and ruin.
Favoring giving leads to undefined portions;
if the superior's portions are undefined,
the subordinates' expectations are endless.
If much is exacted, it makes enemies of the people;
taking little but giving much,
the measure is unsustainable.
Thus, favoring giving
is a way to invite resentment.
From this perspective,
wealth is not reliable to depend on;
the Way's methods can be followed—
this is clear.
Wénzǐ asked:
The ancient kings,
who governed the world with the Dào,
how did they accomplish this?
Lǎozǐ said:
They held fast to the One and practiced non-action,
following the transformations of Heaven and Earth.
"The world is a great vessel,
it cannot be controlled,
it cannot be acted upon.
Those who act upon it ruin it,
those who control it lose it."
Holding fast to the One
means perceiving the subtle.
Perceiving the subtle thus enables one to achieve greatness.
Practicing non-action
means maintaining stillness.
Maintaining stillness thus enables one to be the standard for the world.
Occupying a great position,
be full yet not overflowing;
residing in a high place,
be noble yet not arrogant.
Occupying a great position without overflowing,
being full without deficiency,
residing above without arrogance,
being high without peril.
Being full without deficiency
is the means to long preserve wealth;
being high without peril
is the means to long preserve nobility.
If wealth and nobility do not leave his person,
and emolument reaches to his sons and grandsons,
then the kingly Dào of old
aimed at this.
Lǎozǐ said:
The people have a Dào which they follow together,
and laws which they uphold together.
Righteousness cannot firmly bind them,
authority cannot compel them absolutely.
Therefore, a ruler is established to unify them.
If the ruler holds fast to the One, there is order;
if he is inconstant, there is chaos.
The way of the ruler
is not for taking action,
but for practicing non-action.
The wise do not use their virtue for personal affairs,
the brave do not use their strength for violence,
the benevolent do not use their position for favoritism—
this may be called the One.
The One
is the path of having no enemies,
the root of the myriad things.
If the ruler frequently changes the laws,
and the state frequently changes its ruler,
and people use their positions to pursue their likes and dislikes,
then the responsibilities and fears of those below cannot be adequately managed.
Therefore, if the ruler loses the One,
the chaos is worse than having no ruler at all.
The ruler must hold fast to the One, and only then can he bring the people together.
Wénzǐ asked:
How many kinds of Kingly Dào are there?
Lǎozǐ said:
Only one.
Wénzǐ said:
In ancient times, some ruled by the Dào,
and some ruled by arms.
Why is this not a single way?
He said: Those who rule by the Dào do so through virtue;
those who rule by arms also do so through virtue.
The use of arms has five categories:
there is righteous arms,
responsive arms,
vengeful arms,
greedy arms,
and arrogant arms.
Punishing the violent and rescuing the weak is called righteous;
when an enemy comes against you and you have no choice but to use arms, it is called responsive;
contending over minor matters, unable to control one's heart, is called vengeful;
coveting others' land,
desiring others' wealth and goods, is called greedy;
relying on the size of one's state,
boasting of the multitude of one's people,
seeking to show superiority over rival states, is called arrogant.
Righteous arms lead to kingly rule,
responsive arms lead to victory,
vengeful arms lead to defeat,
greedy arms lead to death,
arrogant arms lead to destruction.
This is the Dào of Heaven.
Lǎozǐ said:
To abandon the Dào and rely on wisdom is perilous;
to discard method and employ talent leads to hardship.
Therefore, maintain your lot and follow principle.
If you lose, do not worry;
if you gain, do not rejoice.
Success is not something achieved by action;
attainment is not something sought by striving.
What comes in is received, not taken;
what goes out is given, not bestowed.
Life comes because of spring;
death comes because of autumn.
For what is born, feel no gratitude;
for what is killed, feel no resentment.
Then you are close to the Dào.
Wénzǐ asked:
How does a king win the joyful hearts
of the people?
Lǎozǐ said:
Be like the rivers and seas, that is all.
"Insipid, without flavor,
yet inexhaustible in use."
Start small and later become great.
"He who wishes to be above the people
must speak humbly to them;
he who wishes to lead the people
must place himself behind them."
Then the world will surely offer him their joyful affection
and advance their benevolence and righteousness,
without harshness.
"Residing above, yet the people do not feel burdened;
standing in front, yet the multitude does not feel harmed;
the world joyfully supports him and does not tire of him."
Even distant lands with different customs,
every flying and crawling creature,
none fails to feel affection.
There is nowhere it does not penetrate,
nowhere it does not reach.
"Therefore, he is esteemed by the world."
Lǎozǐ said:
To cling to the laws of one age
and condemn the customs handed down through generations
is like gluing the pegs while tuning the sè.
The sage
adapts to the times and changes with expediency,
assesses the situation and applies what is appropriate.
When the world changes, affairs transform;
when the times shift, customs alter.
Discuss the age to establish laws;
follow the times to conduct affairs.
The kings of high antiquity
had different laws and measures,
not because they intentionally opposed each other,
but because the demands of the times differed.
Therefore, do not imitate their established laws,
but imitate that by which they made their laws—
moving along with the transformations.
The laws of the sage can be observed,
but the reason for his law-making cannot be traced to its origin.
His words can be heard,
but the reason for his speaking cannot be given form.
The Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors regarded the world lightly,
comprehended the myriad things,
equalized life and death,
unified transformations,
embraced the Dào and extended sincerity,
using it to mirror the circumstances of the myriad things.
Above, they were friends with the Dào;
below, they transformed along with the people.
Now, if you wish to learn their Dào
but do not attain their clarity and purity,
and the rulers of the time cling to their legal texts,
and enforce their statutes and orders,
they will certainly be unable to achieve order.
Wénzǐ asked about governance.
Lǎozǐ said:
Guide them with the Dào,
nurture them with virtue,
do not display your own worthiness,
do not impose with force;
diminish and hold to the One,
have no place for profit,
show nothing desirable,
"square but not cutting,
sharp but not piercing,"
without arrogance or boasting.
Guide them with the Dào and the people will adhere,
nurture them with virtue and the people will submit,
do not display your worthiness and the people will be content,
do not impose with force and the people will remain simple.
Not displaying worthiness
is frugality,
not imposing with force
is humility.
Lower yourself to gather them,
be generous to win them,
frugal to preserve yourself,
humble to secure peace.
Not lowering leads to dispersion,
not nurturing leads to betrayal,
displaying worthiness makes people contend,
imposing force makes people resent.
People dispersing means the state declines,
people betraying means the ruler lacks authority,
contention leads to wrongdoing,
subordinates resenting superiors endangers the throne.
If these four are truly cultivated,
the right path is nearly achieved.
Lǎozǐ said:
The ruler's words are used by subordinates,
subordinates' words are used by the ruler,
the ruler's words are for constant use,
subordinates' words are for expedient use.
Only the sage understands expediency.
Speaking with absolute honesty,
committing with absolute certainty,
are lofty acts in the world,
yet testifying against one's father honestly,
or dying for a woman's trust,
who would value them?
Thus the sage judges right and wrong in matters,
bending and stretching with them,
without fixed standards.
In prayer, name the ruler,
in drowning, grab the father—
circumstances dictate so.
Expediency
is uniquely seen by sages.
First opposing then harmonizing is expediency,
first harmonizing then opposing lacks expediency.
Those lacking expediency
turn good into ugly.
Wénzǐ asked:
Your words imply
without Dào and virtue, one cannot govern the world,
yet ancient kings
inheriting thrones and legacies,
some were without the Dào,
yet died peacefully without disaster—
how is this so?
Lǎozǐ said:
From emperor to commoner,
all live their lives,
but their lives vary in richness.
The world sees states lost and families ruined
due to lack of Dào and virtue.
With Dào and virtue, one toils day and night,
cautious and vigilant,
always fearing peril;
without them, one indulges lazily,
perishing anytime.
Had Jié and Zhòu practiced Dào and virtue,
even Tāng and Wǔ's worthiness
would achieve no merit.
Dào and virtue
enable mutual nurturing,
mutual growth,
mutual affection,
mutual respect.
Even deaf insects, though foolish,
harm not their loved ones;
if all people held benevolent hearts,
how could disasters arise?
Those without Dào yet unharmed
have humanity not fully severed,
righteousness not yet extinguished;
though humanity remains,
though righteousness lingers,
lords already scorn their rulers,
and scorn leads
to disrespect in court,
disobedience to orders.
When humanity severs and righteousness dies,
lords rebel,
masses rely on force,
strong bully weak,
large invade small,
people make conflict their trade,
disasters emerge,
chaos erupts,
ruin is imminent,
how expect no calamity?
Lǎozǐ said:
Harsh laws and penalties breed deceit among people,
many affairs above create many postures below,
seeking much yields little,
prohibiting much overcomes little.
Using affairs to stop affairs
is like fanning flames to prevent burning;
using wisdom to create troubles,
then using wisdom to prepare,
is like stirring water to clear it.
Lǎozǐ said:
If a ruler favors kindness,
the unrewarded get rewards,
the guilty go free;
if he favors punishment,
the meritorious are dismissed,
the innocent executed.
Without preferences,
punishments cause no resentment,
gifts seek no gratitude,
following standards and rules,
self uninvolved in affairs,
like heaven and earth,
why not cover and carry all?
Uniting and harmonizing
is the ruler's role,
distinguishing and punishing
is the law's role.
People accept punishment without resentment,
this is called Dào and virtue.
Lǎozǐ said:
Right and wrong in the world are unsettled,
each age approves what it likes,
disapproves what it dislikes.
Seeking right
is not seeking truth,
but seeking agreement with self;
rejecting wrong
is not rejecting evil,
but removing what offends the heart.
Now I wish to choose right and abide,
choose wrong and avoid,
yet know not the world's so-called right and wrong.
Thus
"governing a large state is like cooking a small fish"—
meaning do not stir.
Those seeking agreement
find words fitting and grow closer,
but if distant yet plans apt,
they are suspected.
Now I wish to correct myself and treat others,
how know how the world spies on me?
If I race with customs,
it's like escaping rain—
nowhere un-wet.
Wanting emptiness,
one cannot be empty;
but not forcing emptiness,
yet naturally empty,
achieves all desires.
Thus one connected to the Dào is like a wheel hub,
not moving itself,
yet with the rim covers a thousand miles,
turning in an endless source.
So the sage embodies Dào, returns to the ultimate,
unchanging to await change,
acting without action.
Lǎozǐ said:
Frequent war with repeated victories
leads the state to ruin,
for frequent war exhausts the people,
repeated victories make the ruler proud.
A proud ruler driving exhausted people
seldom avoids state collapse.
A proud ruler becomes reckless,
recklessness exhausts resources,
exhausted people resent,
resentment breeds extreme schemes.
When both above and below reach extremes,
survival is unheard of.
Thus
"retire when the task is done,
this is the way of heaven."
King Píng asked Wénzǐ:
"I have heard that you attained the Way from Lǎodān,
but now even if a worthy person possesses the Way,
encountering an age of corruption and chaos,
with the authority of just one person,
and wishing to transform long-troubled people,
how could it be possible?"
Wénzǐ replied:
"As for the Way and its Virtue,
it corrects the crooked to make them straight,
calms chaos to bring order,
transforms decadence into simplicity,
so that pure virtue is reborn,
and all under heaven is peaceful and tranquil,
which depends on that one person.
The ruler of men
is the teacher of the people,
those above
are the model for those below,
if those above exemplify beauty, those below will embrace it,
if those above possess the Way and its Virtue, those below will have benevolence and righteousness,
if those below have benevolence and righteousness, then there will be no age of corruption and chaos.
Accumulating virtue leads to kingship,
accumulating resentment leads to ruin,
accumulating stones forms a mountain,
accumulating water forms a sea,
without accumulation yet achieving completion,
such a thing has never existed.
Those who accumulate the Way and its Virtue,
Heaven bestows upon them,
Earth assists them,
spirits and ghosts support them,
phoenixes soar in their courtyards,
qílín roam their outskirts,
and jiǎolóng dwell in their marshes.
Therefore, ruling all under heaven with the Way,
is a blessing to all under heaven,
ruling all under heaven without the Way,
is a curse to all under heaven.
Making one person the enemy of all under heaven,
even if one wishes to endure long,
it cannot be achieved,
Yáo and Shùn thereby prospered,
while Jié and Zhòu thereby perished.
King Píng said:
"I reverently heed your instruction."
Lǎozǐ said:
"The ruler
is the heart of the state,
if the heart is orderly, all parts are at peace,
if the heart is disturbed, all parts are in chaos,
thus when one's heart is orderly,
the limbs are forgotten,
when the state is orderly,
ruler and minister are forgotten by each other.
Lǎozǐ studied with Cháng Cōng,
saw the tongue and understood preserving softness,
looked up at the roof beams,
stepped back and gazed at the river,
observed shadows and understood holding back,
thus the sage is empty, without desire, and follows nature,
always staying behind and not taking the lead,
like stacking firewood for burning,
the last placed ends up on top.
Lǎozǐ said:
"The ringing bell destroys itself with its sound,
the greased candle consumes itself with its light,
the tiger and leopard's patterned fur attracts arrows,
the monkey's agility invites capture,
thus the brave and martial die due to their strength,
the eloquent are trapped by their wit and intelligence.
Able to know through wisdom,
yet unable to not know through wisdom,
thus being skilled in one ability,
perceptive in one argument,
one may discuss specific topics,
but cannot respond broadly.
Lǎozǐ said:
"The Way takes non-being as its substance,
looking at it, its form cannot be seen,
listening to it, its sound cannot be heard,
it is called the dark and obscure.
The dark and obscure
is used to metaphorize the Way,
but it is not the Way itself.
As for the Way,
one looks inward and reflects on oneself,
thus if people are not slightly awakened,
they will not be greatly deluded,
if not slightly wise,
they will not be greatly foolish.
Do not mirror yourself in flowing puddles,
but in still water,
because it maintains its stillness within,
calm and not动荡 outward.
At full moon, the sun's light is overshadowed,
the yīn cannot override the yáng,
when the sun rises, the stars disappear,
unable to compete with its light,
the branch cannot overpower the root,
the limb cannot become larger than the trunk,
if the top is heavy and the bottom light,
it will surely tip over easily.
One deep pool cannot host two jiāo dragons,
one female cannot have two males,
one brings stability,
two bring contention.
With jade in the mountain, plants and trees are moist,
with pearls in the deep, the banks do not wither,
the earthworm lacks strong sinews and bones,
or sharp claws and teeth,
yet it eats dry soil above,
drinks from the underworld springs below,
because its mind is focused.
Clarity brings brightness,
in a cup of water one can see the pupil of an eye,
turbidity causes harm,
in river water one cannot see Tài Mountain,
the orchid and zhǐ do not cease their fragrance for not being worn,
a boat on river or sea does not sink for not being ridden,
the nobleman practicing the Way does not stop for not being recognized,
it is in their nature.
Entering turbidity with clarity leads to hardship and disgrace,
entering clarity with turbidity leads to overthrow and collapse,
when heaven has two qì, a rainbow forms,
when earth has two qì, its stores leak away,
when humans have two qì, illness arises,
yīn and yáng cannot be constant,
alternating winter and summer,
the moon does not know the day,
the sun does not know the night.
Wide rivers breed large fish,
high mountains grow tall trees,
broad lands foster thick virtue,
thus fish cannot be caught without bait,
animals cannot be lured with empty traps.
Where mountains have fierce beasts,
the trees are left uncut,
where gardens have stinging insects,
the mallows are left unharvested,
where the state has worthy ministers,
they repel enemies a thousand miles away;
those who comprehend the Way are like a cart's axle,
turning within the hub,
not moving by themselves,
yet reaching a thousand miles with it,
ending and beginning anew,
turning in the source of infinity.
Thus, aligning with the crooked and the straight,
how can one not obtain,
aligning with the straight and the crooked,
do not follow along."
A bird is about to come,
so one sets a net to await it.
The one that catches the bird is but one mesh of the net.
If one were to make a net of just one mesh,
one would never catch a bird.
Thus, events may not always follow prior rules,
and things may not be premeditated.
Therefore, the sage nurtures the Way and awaits the right time.
Those who wish to attract fish first clear the valley streams;
those who wish to draw birds first plant trees.
When water accumulates, fish gather;
when trees flourish, birds congregate.
To catch fish,
one does not carry them into the deep;
to capture monkeys,
one does not carry them up the trees—
one merely allows them to follow what benefits them.
Where the foot treads is shallow,
yet it relies on where it does not tread to be able to walk;
what the mind knows is limited,
yet it relies on what it does not know to become enlightened.
When the river dries up, the valley becomes empty;
when the hill is leveled, the abyss is filled;
when the lips are gone, the teeth feel cold;
when the river is deep, the soil remains on the mountain.
Water, when still, becomes clear;
clear, it becomes level;
level, it becomes even;
even, it reveals the forms of things.
Forms cannot be merged,
so they can serve as standards.
What causes leaves to fall
is the wind shaking them;
what makes water turbid
is things disturbing it.
The jade disc and large ring
are the work of the grindstone;
the sharpness of Mòyé's cutting
is due to the power of whetstones.
A gadfly and a steed both travel a thousand li, but the gadfly does not fly;
without provisions for the journey, one does not go hungry.
When the cunning hare is caught, the hunting dog is boiled;
when the high-flying birds are gone, the good bow is stored away.
When fame is achieved and success complete, withdraw from prominence—
such is the way of Heaven.
Anger arises from non-anger,
action emerges from non-action.
Look at what has no form, and you will see what is to be seen;
listen to what has no sound, and you will hear what is to be heard.
Flying birds return to their homeland,
hares run back to their burrows,
foxes die facing their mound,
cicadas cling to trees—
each depends on where it was born.
Water and fire despise each other,
but with a cauldron between them,
the five flavors are harmonized.
Bone and flesh love each other,
but with slanderers coming between,
father and son endanger one another.
Dogs and pigs eat without choosing their food,
fattening their bodies all the more,
thus nearing their death.
The phoenix soars a thousand ren high,
and none can reach it.
A chisel is fixed in its handle,
yet it cannot strike itself;
the eyes can see a hundred paces away,
yet they cannot see their own sockets.
Building a mountain from high ground makes it secure and not perilous;
forming an abyss from low ground draws fish and turtles to it.
Ponds and pools overflow in heavy rain,
but dry up in drought;
the source of rivers and seas is deep and never exhausts.
The turtle has no ears, but its eyes cannot be obscured—
it is refined in sight;
the blind have no eyes, but their ears cannot be obscured—
they are refined in hearing.
Turbid, muddy water
can be used to wash my feet;
clear, cool water
can be used to wash my hat strings.
Fine silk woven into plain cloth
may become a crown
or footcloth.
As a crown, it is worn on the head;
as a footcloth, it is trodden underfoot.
Metal's nature overcomes wood,
yet one blade cannot destroy a whole forest;
earth's nature overcomes water,
yet one handful cannot block a river;
water's nature overcomes fire,
yet one dipper cannot extinguish a cartload of burning firewood.
Thunder in winter,
hail in summer—
cold and heat do not change their course.
Frost and snow pile high,
but melt when the sun rises.
What is tilted is easy to topple,
what leans is easy to push over,
what is subtle is easy to assist,
dampness easily brings rain.
Orchids and angelica are fragrant,
but cannot endure frost;
the toad avoids weapons,
yet its life ends on the full moon of the fifth month.
Those who dissipate their essence easily deteriorate within;
flowers blooming out of season cannot be eaten.
The tongue and the teeth—
which will wear out first?
The cord and the arrow—
which will break first?
What makes a shadow crooked is the form;
what makes an echo harsh is the sound.
One who shares the same ailment as the dying
cannot be a good physician;
one who follows the same path as a fallen state
cannot offer loyal counsel.
Have a performer play the yu,
and a craftsman finger the holes—
though they may keep time,
they cannot be made to decide,
for the ruler of form is lost.
The deaf do not sing,
having no way to enjoy themselves;
the blind do not look,
having no way to perceive things.
Walking through a forest,
one cannot take a straight path;
traveling perilous terrain,
one cannot walk a straight line.
The sea contains all that flows into it,
thus it can be vast.
The sun and moon do not appear together;
a fox does not have two males;
the divine dragon has no match;
fierce beasts do not form herds;
birds of prey do not fly in pairs.
A roof cannot block the sun without its rafters;
a wheel cannot pursue speed without its axle—
yet rafters and wheels alone are not enough to rely on.
Draw a bow to shoot,
but without the string, it cannot release;
releasing the arrow is but one part
of the act of shooting.
A hungry horse in the stable
stands silent and still,
but toss fodder beside it,
and contention arises.
A three-inch pipe without a bottom
cannot be filled by all under heaven;
a ten-dan vessel with a stopper
holds but a hundred dou.
Cut along the marking line, and you will not exceed;
weigh with a suspended balance, and you will not err.
Apply ancient laws by analogy,
and sometimes you will succeed;
rely on rules and measures,
and sometimes they will be implemented.
To act accordingly
is called judgment;
to act contrary
is called chaos.
The farmer toils while the gentleman is nourished,
the foolish speak while the wise select,
when something appears clear,
treat it like jade;
when it seems obscure,
one must reserve judgment.
The brightness of a hundred stars
is not equal to the light of one moon;
ten windows all open
do not match the clarity of one door.
A viper should not be given feet,
a tiger should not be given wings.
Now take a mat six chi long:
lying down to cross it
is easy for the least talented,
but standing to step over it
is hard even for the most gifted—
the circumstances differ.
Those who assist in sacrifices get to taste,
those who intervene in fights get wounded.
Sheltering under an inauspicious tree,
one may be struck by lightning.
The sun and moon wish to shine,
but floating clouds obscure them;
rivers wish to be clear,
but sand and silt muddy them;
orchids wish to grow tall,
but autumn winds wither them;
human nature seeks peace,
but desires harm it.
To want no dust in one's eyes while covered in grime
is an unattainable purity.
Gold seals with turtle knobs
are worn by the virtuous as pendants;
soil spread across the land
is turned to wealth by the capable.
Thus, giving gold and jade to the weak
is不如不如 giving them plain silk.
A hub, hollow yet centered, holds thirty spokes,
each exerting its strength;
if one spoke alone were to enter,
the others would all be discarded—
how could any distance be reached?
Orange and pomelo trees have their homeland,
reeds and rushes their thickets;
beasts with like feet roam together,
birds with like wings fly in flocks.
To wish to survey the lands of the nine provinces
without traveling a thousand li,
or to lack the source of governance and teaching
yet aspire to lead the myriad people—
how difficult!
The reckless are captured,
the conspicuous are shot;
thus,
"The greatest whiteness seems sullied,
the broadest virtue seems insufficient."
The gentleman has wine,
the commoner beats a pottery jar;
though it may not be pleasing,
it can still serve for amusement.
Human nature
favors soft silk garments,
yet in battle, one dons armor—
enduring discomfort
to gain advantage.
Thirty spokes share one hub,
each fitting into its own mortise,
unable to interchange,
just as ministers each uphold their duties.
Those skilled in employing people
are like the legs of a millipede,
numerous yet not hindering each other,
or like the tongue and teeth,
hard and soft grinding together without harm.
Stones are hard from birth,
angelica is fragrant from growth;
possessing these traits young,
they grow even brighter with age.
Supporting and lifting,
thanking and yielding,
gaining and losing,
promising and refusing—
they are a thousand li apart.
What grows twice will not be harvested;
what blooms too early falls without frost.
Smearing the nose bridge,
powdering the forehead,
with a rotten rat in the corner
and smoke filling the hall,
then entering water and hating dampness,
clinging to stench while seeking fragrance—
even the skilled cannot achieve excellence thus.
Winter ice can be broken,
summer wood can be tied,
for time is hard to gain and easy to lose.
When trees are lush,
picking all day sees them regrow;
but when autumn winds bring frost,
they wither overnight.
Set up a target, and arrows gather;
where woods are thick, axes enter—
not because they are summoned,
but by the force of circumstances.
A suckling pup biting a tiger,
a brooding hen fighting a fox—
driven by affection,
they disregard their strength.
Those who wait for reward before saving the drowning
will surely drown for that reward.
A boat can float or sink;
the foolish do not set foot on it.
A steed whipped but not advancing,
pulled but not stopping—
a ruler should not use it to measure distance.
Water may be calm,
but waves will arise;
a scale may be level,
but error exists;
a ruler may be straight,
but deviation occurs.
Without compass and square, one cannot fix circles and squares;
without plumb line, there is no straightening curves.
Those who use tools
must also have the mind for them.
The height of Tài Shān,
doubled, becomes unseen;
the tip of an autumn hair,
gazed upon, can be discerned.
Bamboo and wood contain fire,
but without drilling, they won't burn;
earth holds water,
but without digging, it won't flow.
An arrow's speed
cannot exceed two li;
yet with unceasing half-steps,
a lame turtle covers a thousand li.
Piling clods without stop,
a hill is formed.
By the river, desiring fish,
不如不如 return home and weave a net.
First tune the bow, then seek strength;
first tame the horse, then seek speed;
first establish trust, then seek ability.
A skilled smith cannot melt wood,
a fine carpenter cannot carve ice—
some things are impossible;
how can the gentleman not heed this?
To forbid someone from crossing a river
is possible;
to forbid the river from having waves
is not.
Do not claim innocence
when the pot never falls into the well.
Those who criticize my conduct
wish to befriend me;
those who disparage my goods
wish to trade with me.
One move in chess does not reveal wisdom,
one pluck of a string does not convey sorrow.
Now, a single burning ember
can scorch the finger if touched—
too close;
ten thousand stones ablaze,
yet step ten paces away and survive—
same heat, different accumulation.
Where there is glory and bloom,
there must be worry and decay;
above, silks and satins,
below, hempen clothes.
Great trees have sprawling roots,
high mountains have broad foundations.
Lǎozi said:
A drum does not store sound,
thus it can produce sound;
a mirror does not retain forms,
thus it can reflect forms;
metal and stone have sound,
but do not ring without being struck;
pipes and flutes have music,
but do not sound without being blown.
Therefore, the sage stores within,
not initiating for external things,
controlling when affairs arise,
responding when things arrive.
Heaven's motion never ceases,
ending and beginning anew,
thus it can endure long;
the wheel returns to where it turns,
thus it can reach far;
Heaven's motion never errs,
thus it is without fault.
When heavenly qi descends,
and earthly qi ascends,
yīn and yáng communicate,
all things become equal;
the noble man prevails,
the petty man perishes—
this is the way of heaven and earth.
When heavenly qi does not descend,
and earthly qi does not ascend,
yīn and yáng do not connect,
all things do not flourish;
the petty man gains power,
the noble man perishes,
the five grains do not grow,
and the Dào and virtue are stored within.
The way of heaven
takes from the excess to supplement the deficient;
the way of earth
reduces the high to benefit the low;
the way of spirits
humbles the proud to uplift the humble;
the way of man
is that the abundant do not give;
the way of the sage
is humble, and none can surpass it.
When heaven is bright and sun is bright,
then they can illuminate the four directions;
when ruler is bright and minister is bright,
then the realm is at peace;
with these four brightnesses in the realm,
it can endure long.
To understand what spreads brightness
is to understand its transforming power.
Heaven's Dào is pattern,
earth's Dào is principle,
unity harmonizes them,
time directs them,
thus completing all things—
this is called the Dào.
The great Dào is level and broad,
not far from oneself;
cultivate it in oneself,
and one's virtue becomes genuine;
cultivate it in things,
and one's virtue becomes inexhaustible.
Heaven covers all things,
bestowing its virtue to nurture them,
giving without taking—
thus spiritual essence returns to it;
giving without taking
is the highest virtue,
thus it possesses virtue.
Nothing is higher than heaven,
nothing lower than the marsh;
heaven high and marsh low,
the sage models this,
establishing order between noble and humble,
and the world is settled.
Earth carries all things and nurtures them,
giving and taking,
thus bones return to it;
giving and taking
is the lower virtue,
"the lower virtue does not lose virtue,
thus it is without virtue."
Earth supports heaven,
thus it is stable and tranquil;
earth stable and tranquil,
all things take form;
earth broad and thick,
all things gather;
stable and tranquil, it carries all;
broad and thick, it contains all;
earth's disposition deep and substantial,
waters and springs gather within;
earth's Dào square and vast,
thus it can endure long;
the sage models this,
with virtue that contains all.
When yīn yields to yáng,
all things flourish;
when yáng submits to yīn,
all things are serene.
When things flourish, nothing is left unsupported;
when things are serene, nothing is left unjoyful;
when things are joyful, then all is in order.
Yīn harms things,
yáng restrains itself;
yīn advances while yáng retreats,
petty men gain power,
noble men avoid harm—
such is the way of Heaven.
When yáng energy stirs,
all things relax and find their place.
Thus the sage follows the path of yáng.
Those who comply with things
are complied with by things;
those who oppose things
are opposed by things.
Hence they do not lose the innate nature of things.
When marshes are full,
all things mature in season;
when marshes dry up,
all things wither in season.
Thus if rain and moisture fail,
the world becomes desolate.
Yáng rises and then descends again,
thus becoming the master of all things.
Not persisting forever,
it can end and begin anew.
Ending and beginning anew,
it can endure long.
Being able to endure long,
it becomes the mother of the world.
Yáng energy must accumulate before it can bestow;
yīn energy must gather before it can transform.
There has never been transformation without prior accumulation.
Therefore the sage is cautious about what he accumulates.
When yáng overcomes yīn,
all things grow fat;
when yīn overcomes yáng,
all things decay.
Thus if kings and lords honor the way of yáng, all things flourish;
if they honor the way of yīn, the world perishes.
If yáng does not descend to yīn,
all things fail to mature;
if the ruler does not descend to his ministers,
virtuous transformation cannot proceed.
Thus when the ruler descends to his ministers, he becomes clear-sighted;
if he does not descend to them, he becomes deaf and blind.
When the sun rises from the earth,
all things multiply and thrive;
when kings and lords reside above the people,
they illuminate the Dào and virtue.
When the sun sets into the earth,
all things rest and cease;
when petty men reside above the people,
all things flee and hide.
When thunder moves, all things open;
when rain moistens, all things loosen.
When great men carry out their actions,
they resemble this.
The movements of yīn and yáng have constant rhythms;
the actions of great men do not exhaust things.
When thunder shakes the earth,
all things relax;
when wind sways trees,
grass and trees are damaged.
When great men abandon evil and embrace good,
the people do not move far away.
Thus the people have their comings and goings:
they depart from what is especially bad,
and approach what is slightly better.
If wind does not blow,
fire does not emerge;
if great men do not speak,
petty men have nothing to relate.
Fire's emergence must await fuel;
great men's words must have trustworthiness.
Having trustworthiness and truth,
what endeavor would not succeed?
River waters run deep,
soil remains on mountains,
hills and mounds stand high,
while depths descend into abysses.
When yáng energy peaks,
it transforms into yīn;
when yīn energy peaks,
it transforms into yáng.
Therefore desires should not be fulfilled to the brim,
and joy should not be pursued to the extreme.
In resentment, avoid wicked words;
in anger, avoid showing a harsh countenance—
this is called achieving strategy.
Fire flames upward,
water flows downward;
the way of the sage
seeks according to kind.
If the sage leans toward yáng,
the world harmonizes and unites;
if he leans toward yīn,
the world drowns and sinks.
Lǎozi said:
Accumulating thinness makes thickness,
accumulating lowliness makes height.
The noble man daily strives diligently to achieve splendor,
while the petty man daily frets discontentedly until he meets disgrace.
Although their growth and decline may not yet be visible,
therefore treat goodness as if追赶不上,
and harbor ungoodness as if it were inauspicious.
If one inclines toward goodness,
even errors incur no blame;
if one does not incline toward goodness,
even loyalty attracts censure.
Thus, rather than blame others, blame yourself;
striving to demand from others
is not as good as seeking within yourself.
Reputation summons itself,
appearance displays itself,
name appoints itself,
people govern themselves—
nothing is not of one's own doing.
If you grasp a sharp point to stab,
or hold a blade to strike,
why blame others?
Therefore the noble man is cautious in subtle matters.
All things carry yīn on their backs and embrace yáng in their arms,
blending their energies to achieve harmony.
Harmony dwells in the center;
thus fruit of trees grows from the core,
seeds of grasses grow from the pods,
eggs and embryos develop from the center.
Without egg or womb,
life still requires its time.
If the ground is level, water does not flow;
if weights are equal, the scale does not tilt.
The generation and transformation of things
occur through感应 thus.
Lǎozi said:
When mountains reach their height, clouds and rain gather there;
when waters reach their depth, jiāolóng dragons dwell there;
when noble men reach their Dào, virtuous influence flows from them.
Those who possess hidden virtue will surely receive open reward;
those with concealed good deeds will surely achieve clear fame.
Those who plant millet do not harvest rice;
those who sow enmity receive no return of virtue.
Lǎozi said:
The Dào can be weak,
can be strong,
can be soft,
can be hard,
can be yīn,
can be yáng,
can be obscure,
can be bright,
can envelop heaven and earth,
can respond without fixed method.
To know it shallowly is not to know it deeply;
to know it externally is not to know it internally;
to know it roughly is not to know it exquisitely.
To know it is not to know;
not to know is to know.
Who understands that knowing is not knowing,
and not knowing is knowing?
The Dào cannot be heard;
if heard, it is not It.
The Dào cannot be seen;
if seen, it is not It.
The Dào cannot be spoken;
if spoken, it is not It.
Who understands that the formless gives form to forms?
Therefore
"When all the world knows goodness as goodness,
already there is badness!"
"Those who know do not speak;
those who speak do not know."
Wénzǐ asked:
Can one use subtle words?
Lǎozi said:
Why not?
But only if one knows what words point to?
Those who know what words point to
do not use words to speak.
Those who struggle for fish get wet;
those who chase beasts run fast—
not because they enjoy it.
Thus the ultimate word discards words,
the ultimate action discards action.
Those with shallow knowledge
contend over trifles.
"Words have their ancestor;
affairs have their lord.
It is precisely because of ignorance
that I am not understood."
Wénzǐ asked:
"Is there a method for governing a state?"
Lǎozi said:
"Consider those who pull carts:
the one in front calls out 'yéhū',
and those behind respond to it.
This is the song that encourages strength in cart-pulling.
Even the music of Zhèng, Wèi, Hú, and Chǔ
cannot match its appropriateness.
Governing a state requires ritual,
not eloquent debate.
'When laws and decrees multiply,
thieves and bandits increase.'"
Lǎozi said:
"The Dào has no fixed form yet can serve as the standard,
just as a mountain forest has no specific timber yet can provide timber.
Timber does not match the mountain forest,
the mountain forest does not match the clouds and rain,
the clouds and rain do not match yīn and yáng,
yīn and yáng do not match harmony,
and harmony does not match the Dào.
The Dào
is 'what is called the form of the formless,
the image of the imageless.'
One cannot fully comprehend its meaning,
yet between heaven and earth,
it can mold and transform all things."
Lǎozi said:
"When sages establish teachings and implement governance,
they must examine the beginning and end,
observe the creation and consider its effect.
Thus, when people know writing, virtue declines;
when they know calculation, benevolence declines;
when they know contracts, trust declines;
when they know machinery, sincerity declines.
The sè does not sound itself, yet its twenty-five strings each respond with their own tones;
the axle does not move itself, yet its thirty spokes each rotate with their own force.
Strings have slackness and tightness,
then they can form melodies;
the cart has labor and rest,
then it can reach distant places.
What enables sound
is actually the soundless;
what enables rotation
is actually the non-rotating.
Superior and inferior follow different paths;
governance that seeks ease leads to chaos.
Those in high positions with great Dào are followed;
those handling great affairs with petty Dào meet misfortune.
Petty virtue harms righteousness,
petty goodness harms the Dào,
petty arguments harm governance,
harshness injures virtue.
Great correctness is not dangerous,
so people are easily guided;
perfect governance is leisurely,
so subordinates do no harm;
ultimate loyalty returns to simplicity,
so people have no hypocrisy or concealment."
Lǎozi said:
"When collective punishment laws are established,
the common people resent;
when decrees reducing ranks are issued,
meritorious officials rebel.
Therefore, those who examine the traces of legal documents
do not know the root of order and chaos;
those accustomed to battlefield formations
do not understand the strategy of temple warfare.
The sage sees blessings within multiple barriers,
and considers calamities beyond the obscure.
The foolish are deluded by small gains and forget great harms,
thus some matters benefit in small ways but harm in great ways,
gaining here while losing there.
Therefore, no benevolence is greater than loving people,
no wisdom greater than understanding people.
Loving people means no resentful punishments,
understanding people means no chaotic governance."
Lǎozi said:
"Great as rivers are,
their flooding lasts no more than three days;
fierce winds and violent rain
seldom last past noon and cease momentarily.
Those who accumulate no virtue yet feel no anxiety
will soon perish,
for anxiety leads to prosperity,
while complacency leads to ruin.
Therefore, the skilled
use weakness as strength,
turning calamity into blessing.
'The Dào is empty, yet using it cannot be exhausted.'"
Lǎozi said:
"Tranquility, calmness, and harmony
are human nature;
standards and rules
are the measures for affairs.
Knowing human nature, one nurtures oneself without confusion;
knowing the measures for affairs, one's actions are not chaotic.
Issuing one command,
dispersing without boundary,
unifying all controls
is called the mind;
seeing the root and knowing the branches,
grasping one to respond to ten thousand
is called method;
dwelling while knowing the reason,
acting while knowing the destination,
handling affairs while knowing the means,
moving while knowing when to stop
is called the Dào.
Making people honor and praise oneself
is the power of the mind;
making people despise and slander oneself
is the fault of the mind.
Words spoken from the mouth
cannot be stopped by others;
actions starting nearby
cannot be prevented from reaching far.
Affairs are difficult to accomplish but easy to ruin;
reputations are difficult to establish but easy to destroy.
Ordinary people all轻视 small harms
and treat trivial matters lightly,
thus leading to great disasters.
When calamity arrives,
people generate it themselves;
when blessing comes,
people accomplish it themselves.
Calamity and blessing share the same gate,
benefit and harm are close neighbors.
Unless one is extremely refined,
none can distinguish them.
Therefore, wisdom and consideration
are the gateway to calamity and blessing;
movement and stillness
are the pivot of benefit and harm.
One cannot but examine them carefully."
Lǎozi said:
"People all know the key to order and chaos,
but none know the means to preserve life.
Therefore, the sage assesses the age to undertake affairs,
and推断 affairs to form strategies.
The sage can be yīn or yáng,
can be soft or hard,
can be weak or strong,
moving or resting according to the time,
achieving merit based on resources.
Seeing things depart, he knows their return;
observing unity, he discerns its changes.
When transformation occurs, he provides images;
when movement happens, he responds accordingly.
Thus he practices this throughout life without difficulty.
Therefore, some affairs can be discussed but not implemented,
some can be implemented but not discussed,
some are easy to do but difficult to complete,
some are difficult to complete but easy to ruin.
What can be implemented but not discussed
involves choices;
what can be discussed but not implemented
involves deception;
what is easy to do but difficult to complete
concerns affairs;
what is difficult to complete but easy to ruin
concerns reputation.
These four aspects
are what the sage pays attention to,
and what the perceptive uniquely see."
Lǎozi said:
The Dào is about revering the small and being cautious of the subtle,
acting without missing the opportune moment,
with repeated warnings and heavy precautions,
then calamity does not arise,
not calculating blessings before they come,
but considering misfortunes before they occur.
When the same day is covered in frost,
those who are sheltered are not harmed;
the foolish, if prepared, achieve the same merit as the wise.
Accumulated love becomes blessing,
accumulated hatred becomes disaster.
People all know how to rescue from calamity,
but none know how to prevent calamity from arising.
Preventing calamity from arising is easy,
while applying rescue to calamity is difficult.
Now people do not strive to prevent calamity from arising,
but instead strive to apply rescue to calamity;
even a divine person cannot devise a plan for this.
The origins of calamity and misfortune
are myriad and without fixed direction.
The sage dwells deeply to avoid calamity,
remaining silent and still to await the right time.
Petty people do not know the gateways of fortune and misfortune;
acting, they fall into punishment.
Even if they meticulously prepare,
it is not enough to preserve themselves whole.
Therefore, the superior person first avoids calamity and then pursues benefit,
first distances disgrace and then seeks fame.
Thus, the sage constantly engages in affairs beyond form,
and does not fix his mind on what has already taken shape.
Hence, calamity has no way to arrive,
and neither slander nor praise can taint him.
Lǎozi said:
In the way of an ordinary person,
the heart should be small,
the will should be great,
wisdom should be round,
conduct should be square,
abilities should be many,
affairs should be few.
What is meant by a small heart is
considering calamity before it arises,
guarding against misfortune and being cautious of the subtle,
not daring to indulge one's desires.
A great will
encompasses all states,
unifying diverse customs;
right and wrong converge like spokes,
with the center as the hub.
Round wisdom
has no beginning or end,
flowing in all directions,
deep and never exhausted.
Square conduct
stands upright and unbending,
pure white and untainted;
in poverty, not changing one's principles,
in success, not indulging one's ambitions.
Many abilities
include both civil and military arts,
movement and stillness fitting the proper measure;
in promoting, demoting, abolishing, or establishing,
all are appropriately handled.
Few affairs
means grasping the essential to correspond to the multitude,
holding the simple to govern the vast,
dwelling in stillness to manage agitation.
Thus, a small heart
guards against the subtle;
a great will
embraces everything;
round wisdom
knows all;
square conduct
refrains from certain actions;
many abilities
govern everything;
few affairs
simplify what is held.
Therefore, the sage towards goodness,
does not neglect even the small in practice;
towards faults,
does not leave even the subtle uncorrected.
In action, he does not use shamans or wizards,
yet ghosts and spirits dare not precede him.
He can be called supremely noble,
yet he is trembling and fearful,
daily more cautious,
thus achieving wúwéi and the sincerity of oneness.
The wisdom of a fool
is inherently meager,
yet the affairs he undertakes are many;
therefore, his actions inevitably lead to exhaustion.
Thus, using correct teachings to transform,
the situation is easy and sure to succeed;
using perverse teachings to transform,
the situation is difficult and sure to fail.
Abandoning what is easy and sure to succeed,
and engaging in what is difficult and sure to fail,
is due to foolish delusion.
Lǎozi said:
The rise of blessings is continuous and subtle,
the birth of calamities is separate and distinct.
The principles of fortune and misfortune are subtle and invisible,
but the sage sees their beginning and end,
thus they cannot be unexamined.
The enlightened ruler's rewards and punishments
are not for his own sake,
but for the state's.
What suits himself but brings no merit to the state
receives no reward;
what opposes himself but benefits the state
incurs no punishment.
Thus, one who carries righteousness according to appropriateness is called a noble person;
one who abandons righteousness's appropriateness is called a petty person.
The thoroughly wise attain without toil,
the next toil without distress,
the lowest are distressed and toil even more.
The ancients savored without abandoning,
modern people abandon without savoring.
Zhòu having ivory chopsticks made Jīzǐ weep;
Lǔ burying with figurines made Confucius sigh—
seeing the beginning, they knew the end.
Lǎozi said:
Benevolence is what people admire,
righteousness is what people esteem.
Being admired by others,
being esteemed by others,
yet some meet with personal death or national ruin—
this is due to incompatibility with the times.
Hence, those who know benevolence and righteousness but do not understand worldly power
fail to comprehend the Dào.
The Five Emperors valued virtue,
the Three Kings employed righteousness,
the Five Hegemons relied on force.
Now, to adopt the way of the emperors and kings
and apply it in the age of the hegemons
is not the right Dào.
Thus, good and bad are the same,
blame and praise depend on customs;
aims and actions are equal,
adversity and favor lie in the timing.
Knowing what Heaven does,
and knowing what humans do,
then one has the means to manage the world;
knowing Heaven but not knowing humans,
one has no way to interact with customs;
knowing humans but not knowing Heaven,
one has no means to wander with the Dào.
Straightforward will and indulgent emotions
are harmed by stubbornness;
letting the body be enslaved by things,
one is consumed by yīn and yáng.
Those who have attained the Dào
transform outwardly but do not transform inwardly.
Outward transformation is how they understand people;
inward non-transformation is how they preserve themselves.
Thus, internally they have steadfast integrity,
while externally they can bend and stretch,
moving along with things,
acting myriad times without falling into traps.
What is valued about the Dào
is its dragon-like transformation.
Sticking to one principle,
promoting one conduct,
even if successful and full, is still inflexible,
constrained by minor preferences and blocked from the great Dào.
The Dào
is silent and empty,
not acting upon things,
nor acting for itself.
Therefore, those who undertake affairs in accord with the Dào
are not acting by the Dào itself,
but are where the Dào is applied.
What Heaven and Earth cover and carry,
what the sun and moon illuminate,
what yīn and yáng warm,
what rain and dew moisten,
what morality supports—
all share the same harmony.
Hence, those who can uphold the great circle tread the great square;
those who mirror the great clarity see the great light;
those who establish great peace reside in the great hall;
those who can wander in the obscure
share the same light as the sun and moon,
the formless born from the formed.
Thus, the true person entrusts their time to the spiritual tower
and returns to dwell in the beginning of things,
seeing into the obscure,
hearing the soundless,
in the obscurity alone having dawn,
in the silence alone having illumination.
Its use is non-use,
only through non-use can it be used;
its knowing is non-knowing,
only through non-knowing can it be known.
The Dào
is what things follow;
virtue
is what supports life;
benevolence
is the evidence of accumulated kindness;
righteousness
is what aligns with the heart and suits the multitude.
When the Dào perishes, virtue rises;
when virtue declines, benevolence and righteousness emerge.
Thus, the highest age had Dào but not virtue,
the middle age preserved virtue but did not cherish it,
the lower age is cautious and fearful of losing benevolence and righteousness.
Hence, the noble person cannot live without righteousness;
losing righteousness means losing the means to live.
The petty person cannot survive without profit;
losing profit means losing the means to survive.
Thus, the noble person fears losing righteousness,
the petty person fears losing profit.
Observing what they fear,
their fortune and misfortune differ.
Lǎozi said:
Sometimes wanting to benefit something
only ends up harming it;
sometimes wanting to harm something
instead benefits it.
Forcing a feverish person to eat hot food,
or a thirsty person to drink cold water—
this is how the masses nourish themselves,
yet it is what good physicians consider illness.
What pleases the eye,
delights the heart—
these are what the foolish consider beneficial,
but those with the Dào avoid.
The sage
first opposes and then harmonizes;
the masses first harmonize and then oppose.
Thus, the gate of fortune and misfortune,
the reversal of benefit and harm—
cannot be unexamined.
Lǎozi said:
Those with merit who deviate from benevolence and righteousness will be suspected;
those with faults who possess benevolence and righteousness will be trusted.
Therefore, benevolence and righteousness
are the constant accord in affairs,
the honored status in the world.
Even if plans succeed and strategies are appropriate,
troubles are considered and the state preserved from danger,
if the actions deviate from benevolence and righteousness,
the merit will not be achieved.
Even if words do not fit the strategy,
the plans do not benefit the state,
but the heart is devoted to the ruler
and aligned with benevolence and righteousness,
the person will surely survive.
Hence, it is said: those whose hundred words and hundred plans often miss the mark
would do better to abandon haste and carefully examine benevolence and righteousness.
Lǎozi said:
Teaching originates from the noble person,
the petty person receives its benefit;
profit originates from the petty person,
the noble person enjoys its fruits.
