If noble and petty persons each attain their proper place,
then exchanging achievements and sustenance, the Dào is realized.
Excessive desires injure righteousness,
excessive worries harm wisdom.
Thus, in a well-governed state,
joy is what preserves it;
in a tyrannical state,
joy is what destroys it.
Water flows downward and becomes vast;
the ruler lowers himself to his ministers and becomes wise.
The ruler not contending with his ministers allows the way of governance to flow.
Hence, the ruler
is the root,
the ministers are the branches and leaves.
If the root is not healthy yet the branches and leaves are lush,
such a thing has never been.
Lǎozi said:
A loving father’s affection for his son
does not seek repayment;
it cannot be unraveled from the heart.
The sage ruler’s nurturing of the people
is not for his own use;
it is an unceasing nature.
But if he relies on their strength,
depends on their achievements, he will surely be thwarted;
having ulterior motives means kindness is not conveyed.
Thus, using what the masses love
gains the strength of the masses;
promoting what the masses enjoy
wins the hearts of the masses.
Therefore, see the beginning,
and you know the end.
Lǎozi said:
People love through righteousness,
factions strengthen through unity.
Hence, where virtue is broadly applied,
there authority reaches far;
where righteousness is thinly spread,
there force controls little.
Lǎozi said:
To obtain something through unrighteous means,
and then not distribute it,
disaster will reach one's person,
unable to act for others,
and having no means to act for oneself,
can be called a foolish person,
no different from an owl doting on its young.
Therefore,
"Grasp it and fill it to the brim,
better to stop in time;
hammer it and sharpen it to a point,
it cannot long endure."
Within virtue there is the Way,
within the Way there is virtue,
their transformations are without limit,
within yang there is yīn,
within yīn there is yáng,
all things are like this,
too vast to be fully illuminated.
When fortune arrives, auspicious signs are present;
when calamity comes, ominous signs appear first.
Seeing auspicious signs but not doing good,
then fortune will not come;
seeing ominous signs but practicing good deeds,
then calamity will not arrive.
Benefit and harm share the same gate,
calamity and fortune are neighbors,
none but the divine and sage can distinguish them.
Hence it is said:
"Calamity is where fortune depends;
fortune is where calamity lurks.
Who knows their ultimate end?"
When a person is about to fall ill,
they must first savor the taste of fish and meat;
when a state is about to perish,
they must first detest the words of loyal ministers.
Thus for a disease nearing death,
one cannot become a good physician;
for a state nearing collapse,
one cannot offer loyal counsel.
Cultivate it in oneself,
then one can govern the people;
manage the household well,
then one can extend this to officials and leaders.
Therefore it is said:
"Cultivate it in oneself,
one's virtue becomes genuine;
cultivate it in the family,
one's virtue becomes abundant;
cultivate it in the state,
one's virtue becomes plentiful."
What sustains the people's livelihood
is clothing and food.
Affairs that provide for clothing and food achieve merit;
those that don't provide for them achieve no merit.
Affairs without merit, virtue does not grow.
Thus following the season without success,
do not change the punishment;
complying with the time without success,
do not alter the principles.
The time will arise again—
this is called the guiding principle of the Way.
Emperors and kings enrich their people;
hegemons enrich their territory;
endangered states enrich their officials.
A well-governed state seems insufficient;
a perishing state has empty granaries.
Hence it is said:
"When those above take no action, the people naturally become prosperous;
when those above practice non-action, the people naturally transform."
Raising an army of a hundred thousand,
daily expenses amount to a thousand gold.
"After military campaigns,
there must be years of calamity."
Therefore,
"Weapons are instruments of ill omen,
not the treasures of a noble person."
"Reconciling great enmity will leave residual resentment."
How can one then act unkindly?
In ancient times, they drew near those close by not through words,
attracted those far away not through speech,
causing the near to be pleased,
and the far to come.
Sharing the same desires with the people leads to harmony;
sharing the same defense with the people leads to firmness;
sharing the same thoughts with the people leads to wisdom.
Gaining the people's strength leads to wealth;
gaining the people's praise leads to renown.
Actions can summon enemies;
words can bring about calamity.
Do not speak before others;
follow after others and stop.
Whispered words close to the ear
can spread a thousand miles—
such is the calamity of speech.
The tongue is a trigger;
once words are spoken improperly,
a team of four horses cannot retrieve them.
In the past, Zhōnghuángzǐ said:
"Heaven has five directions,
earth has five phases,
sound has five notes,
things have five flavors,
colors have five hues,
people have five ranks.
Thus between heaven and earth there are twenty-five types of people.
The upper five include spiritual persons,
perfected persons,
persons of the Way,
ultimate persons,
and sage persons.
The next five include virtuous persons,
worthy persons,
wise persons,
good persons,
and eloquent persons.
The middle five include public-spirited persons,
loyal persons,
trustworthy persons,
righteous persons,
and courteous persons.
The next five include scholars,
artisans,
foresters,
farmers,
and merchants.
The lower five include common people,
servants,
foolish persons,
carnal persons,
and petty persons."
The upper five compared to the lower five
are like humans compared to oxen and horses.
The sage person
sees with the eyes,
hears with the ears,
speaks with the mouth,
and walks with the feet.
The perfected person
sees without looking and is clear,
hears without listening and is sharp,
follows without walking,
and is just without speaking.
Thus what the sage uses to move the world,
the perfected person has never engaged in;
what the worthy person uses to rectify customs,
the sage person has never observed.
What is called the Way
has no front nor back,
no left nor right;
all things are mysteriously one,
without right nor wrong.
Lǎozi said:
Clarity and emptiness
are heaven's brightness;
non-action
is the constant principle of governance.
Discard favors,
relinquish sage wisdom,
keep virtuous talents at a distance,
abolish benevolence and righteousness,
eliminate affairs,
reject flattering rhetoric,
and prohibit deceit and falsity—
then the worthy and unworthy alike align with the Dào.
Stillness brings unity,
emptiness brings penetration;
the highest virtue is non-action,
and all things are accommodated.
The way of emptiness and stillness
endures as long as heaven and earth;
spirit, subtle and all-pervading,
dominates nothing among things.
The twelve months revolve,
cycling and beginning anew;
metal, wood, water, fire, and earth
conflict in their tendencies,
yet their paths interdepend.
Thus, extreme cold harms things,
but without cold, it is not permissible;
extreme heat harms things,
but without heat, it is not permissible.
Hence, the permissible and impermissible are both permissible.
Therefore, the great Dào permits all things;
permissibility lies in its principle.
Seeing the permissible, do not rush toward it;
seeing the impermissible, do not fail to depart.
The permissible and impermissible
serve as left and right,
as surface and interior.
The essence of all affairs
must begin from oneness;
time is their guideline.
From ancient times to the present,
it has never changed—
this is called heavenly principle.
Above, hold the great brightness;
below, use its light.
The Dào gives birth to all things,
ordered by yīn and yáng,
transformed into the four seasons,
divided into the five phases,
each finding its place,
coming and going with time.
Laws and measures have constancy,
reaching down to the incapable;
the way above does not collapse,
and all ministers are of one mind.
The way of heaven and earth is non-action yet complete,
attaining without seeking.
"Thus, we know that non-action is beneficial."
Lǎozi said:
The uncarved block, at its greatest, has no form;
the Dào, at its greatest, has no measure.
Thus, heaven's circle fits no compass,
and earth's square fits no square.
Past and future coming and going is called eternity;
the four directions and up and down are called space.
The Dào is within them, yet none know its location.
Hence, one who sees not far
cannot be spoken to of greatness;
one whose knowledge is not broad
cannot be discussed with about the ultimate.
Those endowed with the Dào and in communion with things
have no grounds to oppose each other.
Thus, the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors had different methods and records,
but their attainment of the people's hearts was one.
As for compass, square, hook, and line,
they are tools of skill,
but not the means to skill itself.
Thus, without strings, even Master Wén could not complete his melody;
with strings alone, he could not evoke sorrow alone.
Hence, strings
are the instruments of sorrow,
but not the cause of sorrow.
As for spiritual harmony,
wandering between heart and hand,
releasing intention to convey spirit,
discussing change and giving form through strings—
this a father cannot teach his son,
nor can a son receive it from his father.
This is the untransmittable Dào.
Thus, desolation is the ruler of form,
and silence is the master of sound.
Lǎozi said:
The way of heaven and earth
takes virtue as its master,
with the Dào as its decree,
and things rectify themselves.
The most subtle lies deep within,
not valuing itself through affairs.
Thus, it stands without awaiting achievement,
is honored without position,
manifests without fame,
is dignified without ritual,
and is strong without arms.
Hence, the Dào is established but does not teach;
it illuminates but does not scrutinize.
The Dào being established without teaching
does not rob people of their abilities;
illuminating without scrutinizing
does not harm their affairs.
Those who teach the Dào
act contrary to virtue
and harm things.
Thus, yīn and yáng, the four seasons,
metal, wood, water, fire, and earth
share the same Dào but differ in principle;
all things share the same essence but differ in form.
The wise do not teach each other,
the capable do not impart to one another.
Hence, the sage establishes laws
to guide the people's hearts,
letting each follow their nature.
Thus, the living hold no virtue,
and the dead bear no resentment.
"Heaven and earth are not benevolent,
treating all things as straw dogs;
the sage is not benevolent,
treating the people as straw dogs."
Compassion, love, benevolence, and righteousness
are narrow paths.
The narrow-minded enter the vast and get lost;
the short-sighted travel far and become confused.
The way of the sage
enters the vast without getting lost,
travels far without confusion,
constantly empty and self-contained,
able to reach the ultimate—
this is called heavenly virtue.
Lǎozi said:
The sage is covered by heaven, supported by earth,
illumined by the sun and moon,
harmonized by yīn and yáng,
transformed by the four seasons,
embracing all things without partiality,
without old or new,
without distance or intimacy,
thus able to emulate heaven.
Heaven does not have one season,
earth does not have one resource,
humans do not have one affair.
Hence, endeavors are manifold,
and pursuits diverse.
Thus, in employing troops,
some are light, some heavy,
some greedy, some honest—
these four are opposites,
yet none can be absent.
The light wish to advance,
the heavy wish to hold back;
the greedy wish to seize,
the honest do not profit from what is not theirs.
Hence, the brave can be ordered to advance and fight,
but not to hold firm;
the heavy can be ordered to defend steadfastly,
but not to assault the enemy;
the greedy can be ordered to attack and capture,
but not to distribute wealth;
the honest can be ordered to keep to their duty,
but not to take initiative;
the trustworthy can be ordered to uphold agreements,
but not to adapt to change.
These five types
the sage employs together, utilizing their talents.
Heaven and earth do not cherish one thing,
yīn and yáng do not produce one kind.
Thus, the sea does not refuse floods to achieve its greatness;
mountains and forests do not refuse twisted trees to achieve their loftiness;
the sage does not decline the words of firewood carriers to broaden his fame.
To cling to one corner and neglect all others,
to take one thing and discard the rest,
means what is gained is meager,
and what is governed is shallow.
Lǎozǐ said:
Under the canopy of heaven,
upon the support of earth,
and within the illumination of the sun and moon,
forms differ and natures vary,
each finding its own place of comfort;
that which is taken for joy
is precisely what leads to sorrow,
and that which is considered secure
is exactly what becomes perilous.
Thus, when the sage nurtures and governs the people,
he enables each to follow their nature,
settle in their dwellings,
occupy their suitable positions,
do what they are capable of,
move where they are suited,
and apply what is appropriate to them.
In this way, all things are unified,
with no cause to surpass one another.
In the world of things,
there is no inherent nobility or baseness;
value them for what they hold dear,
and nothing remains unvalued;
disparage them for what they disdain,
and nothing remains undisparaged.
Hence, not exalting the worthy means
not placing fish in trees,
nor submerging birds in deep waters.
In ancient times, when Yáo ruled the world,
Shùn served as Minister of Education,
Xiè as Minister of War,
Yǔ as Minister of Works,
Hòujì as Overseer of Farmlands,
and Xīzhòng as Master of Crafts.
In guiding the people,
those by water fished,
those in forests gathered,
those in valleys herded,
those on plains farmed.
The land suited their tasks,
the tasks suited their tools,
the tools suited their materials.
In marshes, they wove nets;
on hillsides, they plowed fields.
Thus, the people could exchange what they had for what they lacked,
what they were skilled at for what they were clumsy in,
and what they excelled in for what they were short on.
As a result, few rebelled,
and many complied,
like the wind passing over reeds,
suddenly stirring them,
each responding with its clear or turbid note.
Nothing fails to pursue its benefit
and avoid its harm.
Thus, neighboring states were within sight,
the sounds of chickens and dogs within hearing,
yet footsteps did not tread into the territories of other lords,
nor did chariot tracks extend beyond a thousand miles,
for all were content in their dwellings.
Therefore, a chaotic state appears prosperous,
a well-governed state seems empty,
a perishing state seems lacking,
a surviving state seems abundant.
Emptiness does not mean
there are no people,
but that each keeps to their duties;
prosperity does not mean
there are many people,
but that all chase after trivialities;
abundance does not mean
there is great wealth,
but that desires are moderated and affairs are few;
lack does not mean
there are no goods,
but that the people are few and expenses many.
Thus, the laws of the ancient kings
were not created arbitrarily,
but followed natural principles;
their prohibitions and punishments
were not imposed arbitrarily,
but upheld what was essential—
this is the way of superior virtue.
Lǎozi said:
To govern the world with the Dào
is not to alter human nature,
but to follow what people inherently possess and bring it to full expression.
Thus, following leads to greatness,
while forcing action leads to smallness.
In ancient times, those who channeled water
followed its natural flow;
those who cultivated crops
followed the suitability of the land;
those who waged war
followed the desires of the people.
One who can follow thus becomes invincible under heaven.
Things must have their spontaneous nature before human affairs can be properly ordered.
Therefore, when the ancient kings established laws,
they followed human nature to create rituals and regulations.
Without this nature,
people cannot be made to follow teachings;
with the nature
but without the innate capacity,
they cannot be made to follow the Dào.
Human nature possesses the capacity for rén and yì,
yet without the laws created by the sage,
they cannot be directed toward what is right.
By following what people dislike, wrongdoing is prohibited;
thus punishments are not needed,
and authority operates with spiritual power.
Following nature ensures all under heaven obey;
going against nature means laws are established but unused.
The Dào and its virtue
are the foundation of achievement and fame,
what the people cherish.
When the people cherish them, achievement and fame are established.
The ancient rulers who excelled took the rivers and seas as their model.
Rivers and seas do nothing, yet achieve their greatness;
they stay low, thus achieving their vastness.
Therefore they can endure long.
"Being the valley of the world,
their virtue is sufficient."
By doing nothing, they can receive all streams;
by not seeking, they can obtain;
by not acting, they can arrive.
"Thus they gain the world without exertion."
Not esteeming themselves, they become rich;
"not displaying themselves, they become illustrious;
not priding themselves, they become leaders."
Abiding in a position of non-possession,
they become kings of the world.
"Not competing, thus none can compete with them."
"Always remaining small, thus they can achieve greatness."
Rivers and seas are close to the Dào,
therefore they can endure long,
preserved together with heaven and earth.
When kings and lords cultivate the Dào,
"their work is accomplished but they claim no possession."
Not claiming possession makes them strong and firm;
strong and firm, yet not oppressive to others.
Deep in the Dào means deep in virtue;
deep in virtue means achievement and fame are fully realized.
"This is called mysterious virtue,
so profound!
So far-reaching!
It returns with things to their origin."
The world has a beginning,
but none know its principle.
Only the sage can know the reason why.
It is neither male nor female,
neither feminine nor masculine.
It gives birth but does not die;
through it heaven and earth are formed,
yīn and yáng take shape,
and all things are born.
Thus between yīn and yáng,
there is round and square,
short and long,
existence and extinction.
The Dào gives them their destiny,
hidden and silent, doing nothing.
In the mind, it is very subtle;
in the Dào, it is very fitting.
Death and life share the same principle;
the myriad things transform and change,
all converging in the one Dào.
Simplify life, forget death—
then wherever one goes, there is longevity.
Discard affairs and words,
follow non-action.
Guard the Dào meticulously,
and do not dominate over things.
The most subtle has no form;
it is the beginning of heaven and earth.
The myriad things are one with the Dào but differ in form.
The most subtle has no substance,
thus it can pervade and care for all;
the greatest has no outside,
thus it can cover all things;
the finest has no inside,
thus it is valued by all things.
The Dào preserves life;
virtue secures the body.
The measure of the ultimate Dào
is to abandon likes and dislikes,
to have no knowledge or cunning,
to ease the will and harmonize the heart,
so that nothing opposes the Dào.
Heaven and earth unite as one,
divide into two,
oppose and then combine,
so that above and below do not lose each other;
unite as one,
divide into five,
oppose and then combine,
necessarily conforming to the compass and square.
The Dào is the most intimate, it cannot be distanced;
the closest, it cannot be kept afar.
Those who seek it far away
will go and then return again.
Lǎozi said:
The Emperor has a name,
but none know his true nature.
The Emperor values his virtue,
the King upholds his righteousness,
the Hegemon comprehends principles.
The way of the sage,
towards things has no possessiveness.
When the Way narrows, then wisdom is employed;
when virtue is thin, then punishments are used;
when clarity is shallow, then scrutiny is applied.
Employing wisdom leads to internal disorder in the heart;
employing punishments causes resentment between superiors and inferiors;
employing scrutiny means not seeking goodness in serving superiors, which leads to decay.
Therefore, the sage follows heaven and earth in transformation,
his virtue covers like heaven and supports like earth.
When the Way is guided by timeliness,
its nourishment becomes abundant;
abundant nourishment brings order.
Even if there were divine sages,
how could they change this?
Discard mental knowledge,
reduce punishments and penalties,
return to clarity and stillness—
then things will correct themselves.
The Way as a ruler is like a corpse,
solemnly mysterious and silent,
yet the world receives its blessings.
One person covered by it is not overwhelmed;
ten thousand people covered by it are not constrained.
Hence, heavily bestowing favors
is like heavily committing violence—
then the Way is obstructed.
Bestowing favors means distributing gifts;
rewarding richly without merit,
granting high ranks without labor—
then those holding office become negligent in their duties,
and idlers hasten for advancement.
Violence means reckless punishment,
causing death without crime,
where those practicing the Way suffer penalty—
then those cultivating themselves are not encouraged towards goodness,
and evildoers lightly offend superiors.
Thus, bestowing favors produces treachery;
committing violence produces chaos.
The customs of treachery and chaos
are the winds of a perishing state.
Therefore, when the state has punishments, the ruler feels no anger;
when the court has rewards, the king takes no part.
The punished do not resent the ruler,
for the crime deserves it;
the rewarded do not feel grateful to the superior,
for the achievement caused it.
The people know that punishments and rewards come
all from their own actions,
so they strive for achievements and cultivate their tasks,
not accepting gifts from others.
Thus, the court becomes deserted yet without traces,
the fields opened yet without weeds.
Hence,
"In the highest antiquity, people knew they had it."
The way of the true king
lies in acting through non-action,
teaching without words,
clear and still without movement,
settled without shaking,
following and employing subordinates,
holding them accountable without toil.
Plans never miss the mark,
actions never go too far,
words lack ornamentation,
deeds lack ceremony,
advancing and retreating in accordance with the time,
moving and resting following principle.
Neither fondness nor hatred for beauty and ugliness,
neither joy nor anger in rewards and punishments.
Names determine themselves,
categories classify themselves,
affairs arise spontaneously,
nothing issues from oneself.
If you try to regulate them,
you instead estrange them;
if you try to adorn them,
you instead harm them.
The qi of heaven is the hun soul,
the qi of earth is the po soul;
returning to their mystery,
each resides in its abode.
Guard them and do not lose them,
they ascend to connect with Tàiyī.
The essence of Tàiyī
communicates and merges with heaven.
The way of heaven is silently silent,
without form or rule,
vast beyond limits,
deep beyond measure,
constantly transforming with humans,
unattainable by wisdom,
revolving without end,
nurturing like a spirit,
empty and following,
always behind, not ahead.
In hearing and governing,
empty the mind and weaken the will,
clear and bright, not obscured.
Thus, ministers gather like spokes and advance together;
whether foolish, wise, worthy, or unworthy,
none fail to exhaust their abilities.
The ruler gains the means to control ministers;
ministers gain the means to serve the ruler—
this is how a well-governed state becomes enlightened.
Lǎozi said:
To know and love questioning is sagely;
to be brave and love questioning is victorious.
Riding on the wisdom of the multitude, there is nothing one cannot undertake;
using the strength of the multitude, there is nothing one cannot overcome.
Using the strength of the multitude,
even Wū Huò is not enough to rely on;
riding on the momentum of the multitude,
the world is not enough to employ.
Without the power to act appropriately
and not following the principles of the Way,
even a divine sage cannot achieve success.
Therefore, when the sage initiates affairs,
he never fails to use them according to their resources.
One with a single achievement holds a single position;
one with a single ability performs a single task.
If strength surpasses the responsibility,
then the lifter finds it not heavy;
if ability matches the affair,
then the doer finds it not difficult.
The sage combines and uses them all,
hence
"No person is abandoned,
no material is wasted."
Lǎozi said:
What is called non-action
does not mean that when pulled, it does not come,
when pushed, it does not go,
when pressed, it does not respond,
when moved, it does not act,
stubbornly stagnant and not flowing,
clenched in the fist and not scattering.
It means that personal biases do not enter public justice,
cravings do not distort the correct path,
acting in accordance with principle,
establishing achievements based on resources,
pushing the natural momentum,
allowing no room for cunning schemes.
When affairs are accomplished, the self is not boasted;
when merits are achieved, fame is not claimed.
As for using boats on water,
sledges on sand,
skids on mud,
carts on mountains,
canals in summer, ponds in winter,
building mounds where it is high,
digging pools where it is low—
these are not what I call action.
The sage is not ashamed of his lowly status,
but dislikes the Way not being practiced;
he does not worry about his short life,
but worries about the poverty of the people.
Therefore, he is always empty and acts through non-action,
embracing simplicity and appearing plain,
not mixing with things.
Lǎozi said:
The ancient establishment of emperors and kings
was not to indulge their desires;
the sages ascending the throne
was not for the ease and pleasure of their bodies.
For the people under heaven,
the strong bullied the weak,
the many oppressed the few,
the cunning deceived the foolish,
the brave encroached upon the timid;
furthermore, those who possessed wisdom did not use it to teach others,
and those who accumulated wealth did not share it.
Therefore, the Son of Heaven was established to unify them.
As the vision of one person
cannot illuminate the entire realm,
the three lords and nine ministers were established to assist him.
Because distant lands with different customs
could not receive his beneficence,
feudal lords were established to instruct them.
Thus, heaven and earth and the four seasons all respond accordingly;
no official affairs remain concealed,
no state benefits are neglected,
so that the cold are clothed and the hungry fed,
the elderly and weak are cared for,
the weary and tired are rested—
all is accomplished without exception.
Shénnóng was haggard in form,
Yáo was emaciated,
Shùn was dark and swarthy,
Yǔ had calloused hands and feet,
Yī Yǐn carried a tripod to seek out Tāng,
Lǚ Wàng wielded a butcher’s knife to enter the service of Zhōu,
Bǎilǐ Xī was sold into servitude,
Guǎn Zhòng was bound in fetters,
Kǒngzǐ had no soot-blackened chimney,
Mòzǐ no warm seat—
not because they coveted salaries or admired positions,
but because they sought to promote the benefits of the world
and eliminate the harms to the myriad people.
From the Son of Heaven down to the commoners,
those whose four limbs do not toil,
whose thoughts are not wearied,
yet seek sufficiency in affairs—
such have never been heard of.
Lǎozi said:
What is called the Son of Heaven
possesses the Way of Heaven to establish the world.
The Way to establish the world
holds to Oneness as its safeguard,
returns to the root in non-action,
is empty, tranquil, and without being,
indistinct and without bounds,
distant and without end,
looking at it, it has no form,
listening to it, it has no sound—
this is called the classic of the Great Way.
Lǎozi said:
Now the Way
embodies the circle and follows the square,
turns its back to yīn and embraces yáng,
is soft on the left and firm on the right,
treads in darkness and wears brightness,
changes and transforms without constancy,
attains it from one source,
and responds without fixed direction—
this is called divine clarity.
Heaven is round and without seams,
so its form cannot be seen;
Earth is square and without borders,
so its gate cannot be peered into;
Heaven transforms and nurtures without shape,
Earth gives birth and grows beyond measure.
Now things have their victories,
only the Way has no victory;
the reason it has no victory
is because it has no constant form or situation,
revolving endlessly,
like the movement of the sun and moon,
or the succession of spring and autumn,
the day and night of sun and moon,
ending only to begin again,
brightening only to darken again,
shaping forms without form itself,
thus achievements can be completed;
it things things but is not a thing itself,
thus it prevails without being subdued.
Those who win at the temple become emperors,
those who transform spiritually become kings;
winning at the temple means modeling the Way of Heaven,
spiritual transformation means understanding the four seasons,
cultivating correctness within the borders,
and distant lands embrace their virtue,
achieving victory before battle,
and the feudal lords submit as guests.
The ancient ones who attained the Way
in stillness modeled heaven and earth,
in movement followed the sun and moon,
their joy and anger mirrored the four seasons.
Their commands rivaled thunder,
their voices and breath did not contradict the eight winds,
their bending and stretching did not violate the five measures.
Following the people’s desires,
riding on the people’s strength,
they removed cruelty and eliminated harm for them.
Those who share benefits die for each other,
those who share feelings complete each other,
those who share actions assist each other;
acting in accordance with themselves,
the world fights for them.
Therefore, those skilled in using troops
use them for their own purposes;
those unskilled in using troops
use them for their own personal ends.
Using them for their own purposes,
there is none in the world who cannot be used;
using them for one’s own ends,
not a single person can be used.
Lǎozi said:
In governing the body,
the highest is to nurture the spirit,
the next is to nurture the form.
When the spirit is clear and the mind calm,
all joints are at peace—
this is the root of nurturing life;
fattening the skin and muscles,
filling the belly and intestines,
indulging cravings and desires—
this is the branch of nurturing life.
In governing the state,
the highest is to nurture transformation,
the next is to enforce laws.
When people yield and contend to take the humble position,
compete to receive less wealth and profit,
strive to undertake labor in affairs,
daily transformed by their superiors and moving toward goodness,
without knowing how it is so—
this is the root of governance;
encouraging goodness with rewards and benefits,
fearing punishment and not daring to do wrong,
laws and decrees rectified above,
the common people submitting below—
this is the branch of governance.
The highest age nurtured the root,
while later ages attended to the branch.
Lǎozi said:
A ruler capable of governing does not appear in every generation,
ministers fit to govern with him are not one in ten thousand;
seeking the one-in-ten-thousand with the not-in-every-generation,
this is why perfect governance does not arrive once in a thousand years.
The achievements of hegemons and kings are not established in every age.
Follow their good intentions,
guard against their wicked thoughts,
and share the same path with the people—
then the people can be made good,
and customs can be beautified.
What is valued in the sage
is not valuing his following crimes with punishments,
but valuing his knowing whence disorder arises.
If one opens the sharp edge
and allows them to follow recklessness, depravity, and excess,
then abandons them with laws
and follows with punishments,
even devastating the world cannot stop their treachery.
Lǎozi said:
When the body dwells above the rivers and lakes,
but the mind remains below the palace gates,
this is valuing life;
valuing life means lightening profit.
If still unable to master oneself,
then follow it—
the spirit will not be harmed;
if unable to master oneself
and forcibly not following,
this is called double injury;
a doubly injured person
will not live long.
Therefore it is said:
"Knowing harmony is called constancy,
knowing constancy is called clarity,
enhancing life is called auspicious,
the mind driving the breath is called forcing,"
"this is called mysterious unity,"
"use its light,
return to its clarity."
Lǎozi said:
Under heaven, nothing is easier than doing good,
and nothing is harder than doing evil.
What is meant by doing good being easy is that
one remains tranquil and acts without effort,
satisfies one's nature and discards excess,
is free from all temptations,
follows one's nature and preserves genuineness,
and remains unchanged within oneself;
thus it is said that doing good is easy.
What is meant by doing evil being hard is that
usurpation, murder, arrogance, and licentiousness,
restlessness and excessive desires,
are not part of human nature;
thus it is said that doing evil is hard.
Now, what is considered a great trouble
arises from the lack of constant contentment and measure;
therefore, in the realm of advantage and harm,
at the boundary of misfortune and fortune,
one must be discerning.
The sage has no desires,
no aversions;
if one desires something,
it may lead to losing it;
if one avoids something,
it may lead to encountering it.
When the will has desires,
one forgets what one is doing;
thus the sage carefully examines the changes in movement and stillness,
appropriately applies the measure of giving and receiving,
manages the emotions of likes and dislikes,
and harmonizes the rhythms of joy and anger.
When movement and stillness are proper, troubles do not invade;
when giving and receiving are appropriate, guilt does not accumulate;
when likes and dislikes are managed, worries do not approach;
when joy and anger are harmonized, resentment does not offend.
One who embodies the Dào
does not seek unjust gains,
does not shun misfortune;
what one has is not abandoned,
what is not one's own is not seized;
always full yet not overflowing,
constantly empty yet easily satisfied.
Thus, by measuring with the Dào and methods,
one eats to fill emptiness,
clothes to ward off cold,
and warms and fills the seven-foot body;
without the Dào and methods to measure,
and instead seeking honor and nobility for oneself,
even the power of ten thousand chariots is not enough for pleasure,
and the wealth of the world is not enough for joy.
Therefore, the sage's heart is calm and will easy,
spirit guarded within,
and things cannot confuse him.
Lǎozi said:
"He who conquers others has power;
he who conquers himself is strong."
One who can be strong
must use the strength of others;
one who can use the strength of others
must win the hearts of the people;
one who can win the hearts of the people
must have self-attainment;
there has never been one who attained oneself yet lost others,
nor one who gained others yet lost oneself.
Thus, the root of governance
lies in pacifying the people;
the root of pacifying the people
lies in sufficiency of resources;
the root of sufficiency of resources
lies in not disrupting the seasons;
the root of not disrupting the seasons
lies in reducing affairs;
the root of reducing affairs
lies in frugality;
the root of frugality
lies in eliminating arrogance;
the root of eliminating arrogance
lies in emptiness and non-being.
Therefore, one who understands the nature of life
does not strive for what life cannot achieve;
one who understands the nature of destiny
does not strive for what knowledge cannot change.
The eyes delight in the five colors,
the mouth savors flavors,
the ears indulge in the five sounds;
the seven apertures contend with each other,
harming the one nature.
Daily indulging in evil desires exhausts one's natural harmony;
if one cannot even govern one's own body,
how can one govern the world!
What is called gaining the world
does not mean occupying a position of power
or bearing a title of honor,
but rather moving the hearts of the world,
gaining the strength of the world.
Having the name of a ruler
but not the praise of a single person—
this is to lose the world.
Thus, Jié and Zhòu are not considered kings,
and Tāng and Wǔ are not considered usurpers.
Therefore, when the Son of Heaven attains the Dào,
his defense lies with the four barbarians;
when the Son of Heaven loses the Dào,
his defense lies with the feudal lords.
When the feudal lords attain the Dào,
their defense lies within their four borders;
when the feudal lords lose the Dào,
their defense lies with their attendants.
Thus it is said: do not rely on others not taking from you,
but rely on your own inviolability.
Practicing a way that can be taken from you
while condemning usurpation and murder
is of no benefit in holding the world.
Lǎozi said:
One who is good at governing a state
does not change its past,
nor alter its constants.
For anger is contrary to virtue,
weapons are instruments of misfortune,
and contention is what brings chaos to people.
Plotting against virtue,
fondness for using instruments of misfortune,
and governing people's chaos
are the height of perversity.
Without harming others, one cannot create harm.
"It is better to blunt the sharpness,
untangle the knots,
soften the glare,
and merge with the dust."
Human nature desires to be superior to others and hates being inferior;
desiring to be superior gives rise to a contentious heart,
hating inferiority gives rise to resentment and strife;
when resentment and strife arise, the heart is disordered and the qì rebellious.
Thus, the ancient sage kings eliminated contention and resentment;
when contention and resentment do not arise, the heart is ordered and the qì harmonious.
Therefore it is said:
"Do not exalt the worthy,
and the people will not contend."
Lǎozi said:
To govern things,
do not use things but use harmony;
to govern harmony,
do not use harmony but use people;
to govern people,
do not use people but use the ruler;
to govern the ruler,
do not use the ruler but use desires;
to govern desires,
do not use desires but use nature;
to govern nature,
do not use nature but use virtue;
to govern virtue,
do not use virtue but use the Dào.
With the Dào as the root of nature,
there is no evil or impurity;
long immersion in things makes one forget the root
and merge with what seems like nature.
Clothing, food, rituals, and customs
are not part of human nature;
they are received from without.
Thus, human nature desires peace,
but cravings and desires harm it.
Only those who have the Dào can discard things and return to themselves.
Having self-reflection,
one does not lose the essence of things;
without self-reflection,
one acts and is confused and troubled.
Indulging desires loses nature;
actions are never correct.
Using this to nurture life leads to loss of self;
using this to govern the state leads to chaos among people.
Thus, those who do not understand the Dào
cannot return to their nature.
The ancient sages could attain within themselves,
hence their orders were followed and prohibitions heeded.
In all undertakings,
one must first calm the mind and clarify the spirit;
when the spirit is clear and the mind calm,
things can then be rectified.
If hearing is lost in praise and blame,
and eyes are captivated by colors,
then wanting to rectify affairs is difficult;
thus emptiness is valued.
Just as stirred water produces waves,
disordered qì leads to clouded wisdom;
clouded wisdom cannot rectify things,
and wavy water cannot be level.
Therefore, the sage king holds to the One
to manage the nature and essence of things.
The One
is supremely noble and unmatched under heaven;
the sage king relies on what has no peer,
thus issuing commands for the world.
Lǎozi said:
Yīn and yáng forge all things,
all riding on a single breath to be born.
When superiors and inferiors are of divided heart,
the breath then steams upward,
when ruler and minister are not in harmony,
the five grains do not ripen,
spring is stern and autumn flourishes,
winter thunders and summer frosts,
all are born of thieving breath.
Between heaven and earth,
it is like one person's body,
within the six directions,
it is like one person's form,
thus those who understand nature,
heaven and earth cannot coerce,
those who examine correspondences,
monstrous things cannot confuse.
The sage knows the distant from the near,
taking myriad differences as one unity,
the breath steams through heaven and earth,
ritual, righteousness, integrity, and shame are not established,
the myriad people do not invade or violently oppress one another,
because they exist within the混沌冥昧之中.
When integrity and shame decline,
reaching the decay of the age,
expenditures are many and wealth is scarce,
labor is toilsome and sustenance insufficient,
the people are impoverished and bitter, and resentful strife arises,
thus humanity is valued.
When people are base and not uniform,
forming cliques and factions,
each promoting their associates,
harboring minds of cunning machinery and deceit,
thus righteousness is valued.
When men and women live in groups,
mixed without distinction,
thus ritual is valued.
When the essence of life and nature,
becomes excessive and presses upon one another unavoidably,
leading to disharmony,
thus music is valued.
Therefore humanity, righteousness, ritual, and music,
are means to rescue decay,
not the way of comprehensive governance.
If indeed one can settle the divine and bright throughout the world,
and the mind returns to its origin,
then the people's nature is good,
the people's nature being good, heaven, earth, yīn, and yáng follow and embrace them,
thus wealth is sufficient and people are provided for,
and minds of greed, baseness, and resentful strife do not arise.
Humanity and righteousness are not used,
and the Dào and virtue are settled throughout the world,
and the people are not excessive in colors,
thus when virtue declines, then humanity and righteousness are adorned,
when harmony is lost, then sounds are tuned,
when ritual becomes excessive, then appearances are adorned.
Therefore, knowing the Dào and virtue,
then one knows that humanity and righteousness are not worth practicing,
knowing humanity and righteousness,
then one knows that ritual and music are not worth cultivating.
Lǎozi said:
The governance of clarity and stillness,
is harmonious and compliant in solitude,
genuine in substance and simple in nature,
leisurely and still without agitation,
inwardly conforming to the Dào,
outwardly aligning with righteousness;
its words are concise and follow reason,
its actions are pleasant and accord with feeling,
its heart is harmonious and without falsity,
its affairs are plain and unadorned;
not planning the beginning,
not discussing the end,
at ease then stay,
stirred then go,
the whole body connected with heaven and earth,
the essence one with yīn and yáng,
harmonized with the four seasons,
bright and clear as the sun and moon,
being human with the creator,
cunning machinery and deceit have no place in the heart.
Thus heaven covers with virtue,
earth supports with music,
the four seasons do not lose their order,
wind and rain do not bring disaster,
sun and moon are clear and still, radiating light,
the five planets do not stray from their courses,
this is what clarity and stillness make evident.
Lǎozi said:
In a well-governed age, offices are easy to hold,
affairs are easy to manage,
rituals are easy to perform,
responsibilities are easy to fulfill.
Thus people do not hold multiple offices,
offices do not cover multiple affairs,
farmers, scholars, artisans, merchants,
distinguished by village and separated by region,
so farmers speak with farmers about storage,
scholars with scholars about conduct,
artisans with artisans about skill,
merchants with merchants about calculation.
Thus scholars have no neglected conduct,
artisans have no shoddy work,
farmers have no wasted effort,
merchants have no lost goods,
each secure in their nature.
Different forms and various kinds,
changing affairs without conflict,
losing their occupation, they become lowly,
achieving their aims, they become noble.
Those with foresight and distant vision,
are of abundant talent,
but in a well-governed age, this is not demanded of the people,
extensive learning and strong memory,
eloquent speech and ready words,
are excesses of human knowledge,
and an enlightened ruler does not seek these from below;
disdaining the world and belittling things,
not following the common customs,
are the haughty conduct of scholars,
and in a well-governed age, these are not used to transform the people.
Therefore, what is too high to reach,
is not made the measure for people,
conduct that cannot be matched,
is not made the custom of the state,
thus human talent cannot be exclusively employed,
but measures and methods of the Dào can be passed down through generations.
Thus state laws can be upheld even by the foolish,
and armies can be unified by laws,
without waiting for the heroes of antiquity,
and people are self-sufficient,
because they use what they have to the full.
The laws of a declining age,
set the standard high and punish those who fall short,
make responsibilities heavy and penalize those who cannot bear them,
set dangers as difficulties and execute those who dare not face them,
the people, distressed by these three demands,
then adorn their wisdom to deceive superiors,
commit evils and engage in dangers,
even with severe laws and harsh punishments,
their treachery cannot be prohibited.
A beast cornered will butt,
a bird cornered will peck,
a person cornered will deceive,
this is what it means.
Lǎozǐ said:
The sound of thunder can be represented by bells and drums,
the changes of wind and rain can be known through musical tones,
what is grandly visible
can be measured,
what is clearly apparent
can be concealed,
sounds that can be heard
can be harmonized,
colors that can be discerned
can be distinguished.
As for the supremely great,
heaven and earth cannot contain it;
the supremely minute,
even divine intelligence cannot comprehend it.
When it comes to establishing pitch standards and calendars,
distinguishing the five colors,
differentiating the clear and turbid,
tasting the sweet and bitter,
then the uncarved block disperses and becomes vessels.
Establishing benevolence and righteousness,
cultivating rites and music,
then virtue shifts and becomes artifice.
The people adorn their wisdom to startle the foolish,
set up deceit to attack their superiors;
in the world, there are those who can maintain it,
but none who can truly govern it.
When wisdom and capability multiply,
virtue increasingly decays.
Therefore, the perfect person remains simple and undispersed.
Lǎozǐ said:
The governance of the perfect person
is empty and silent,
not displaying what is desirable,
with the heart dwelling with the spirit,
the body harmonized with nature,
tranquil yet embodying attainment,
active yet penetrating principle,
following the way of spontaneity,
acting only when compelled.
Indifferent and non-acting, yet all under heaven is harmonious;
detached and without desire, yet the people remain simple of themselves.
Without contentious strife, yet wealth is sufficient;
those who give do not claim virtue,
those who receive do not decline,
virtue intermingles and returns,
yet none bestow favor.
The disputation without words,
the way that is not spoken,
if one somehow penetrates it,
it is called the celestial storehouse.
Take from it without depletion,
draw from it without exhaustion,
none know whence it emerges;
it is called the Shaking Light,
the Shaking Light
is what provisions the myriad things.
Lǎozǐ said:
Heaven cherishes its essence,
earth cherishes its balance,
humans cherish their emotions.
Heaven's essence
is the sun, moon, stars,
thunder, wind, and rain;
earth's balance
is water, fire, metal, wood, and earth;
human emotions
are thought, wisdom, hearing, joy, and anger.
Therefore, close the four passes,
halt the five flights,
and you merge with the Way.
Divine intelligence is hidden in formlessness,
vital energy returns to the genuine.
Eyes are bright but not used for seeing,
ears are acute but not used for hearing,
mouth is apt but not used for speaking,
mind is orderly and penetrating but not used for thinking.
Yielding yet not acting,
knowing yet not boasting,
straightening the nature of life,
so that cunning cannot harm.
When essence resides in the eyes, their vision is clear;
when it resides in the ears, their hearing is acute;
when it remains in the mouth, its speech is apt;
when it gathers in the heart, its thoughts penetrate.
Therefore, close the four passes and be without trouble for life.
The four limbs and nine orifices
neither die nor are born;
this is called the genuine person.
Earth's production of wealth
is fundamentally based on the five phases;
the sage regulates the five phases,
thus governing without disorder.
Lǎozǐ said:
When weighing left and right,
impartial to light and heavy,
thus it can be balanced;
when measuring inside and out,
impartial to crooked and straight,
thus it can be correct.
When the ruler applies laws,
impartial in likes and dislikes,
thus they can be commands.
Virtue finds no place to establish,
resentment finds no place to hide;
this is entrusting to the Way and abandoning the human heart.
Therefore, in governing,
knowledge has no part in it.
Water's turbulence wrecks boats,
wood's impact breaks axles;
one does not blame the wood or stone but faults skill or clumsiness,
for knowledge does not bear it.
Thus, when the Way has knowledge, there is chaos;
when virtue has a heart, there is peril;
when the heart has eyes, there is dizziness.
Now scales, weights, compasses, and squares,
once set do not change,
constantly uniform and not deviant,
acting squarely without lingering,
once formed in a day,
passed down for ten thousand generations—
this is the action of non-action.
Unity is non-action,
used by a hundred kings,
handed down for ten thousand generations,
acting without change.
Lǎozǐ said:
People say:
"A state may have a perished ruler,
but the world never loses the Way;
humans may be impoverished, but principle is never blocked."
Therefore, non-action
is the ancestor of the Way.
Grasping the ancestor of the Way,
one responds to the boundless.
Thus, not following the numbers of the Way and principle,
but relying solely on one's own abilities,
one's exhaustion is not far off.
That a ruler does not leave his door yet knows all under heaven
is because he recognizes things through things,
knows people through people.
Therefore, what is lifted by accumulated strength
is never not overcome;
what is done by the wisdom of the multitude
is never not accomplished.
A crowd of a thousand does not lack food;
a group of ten thousand does not waste effort.
Artisans have no different skills,
officials no overlapping duties;
each keeps to their role,
not interfering with others.
People find what suits them,
things find where they rest.
Thus, tools are not crude,
duties are not neglected.
Small debts are easily repaid,
few duties easily maintained;
light responsibilities are easily encouraged.
The superior holds to sparse measures,
the subordinate performs easily achievable tasks;
thus, ruler and minister do not weary of each other.
Lǎo zǐ said:
The Emperor embodies the Great Unity,
the King models on Yīn and Yáng,
the Hegemon follows the four seasons,
the Ruler employs the six pitch-standards.
Those who embody the Great Unity
understand the nature of Heaven and Earth,
comprehend the principles of Dào and Dé,
their intelligence illuminates like the sun and moon,
their spirit connects with all things,
their movements and stillness harmonize with Yīn and Yáng,
their joy and anger accord with the four seasons,
their coverage and dew are all Dào,
impartial and without selfishness,
even the flying and crawling insects
all look up to their Dé and live,
their Dé flows beyond borders,
their fame is passed down to later generations.
Those who model on Yīn and Yáng
inherit the harmony of Heaven and Earth,
their Dé equals that of Heaven and Earth,
their brightness shines alongside the sun and moon,
their spirit is as numinous as ghosts and gods,
they bear the round and tread the square,
hold the standard and rest by the line,
internally they can govern themselves,
externally they win people's hearts,
issuing commands and decrees,
the world follows like the wind.
Those who follow the four seasons
give birth in spring and grow in summer,
harvest in autumn and store in winter,
taking and giving have moderation,
income and expenditure have measure,
joy and anger, firmness and softness,
do not deviate from their principles,
soft but not brittle,
firm but not harsh,
broad but not unrestrained,
stern but not perverse,
gentle and compliant,
to nurture all kinds,
their Dé includes the foolish and tolerates the unworthy,
without any private favor.
Those who employ the six pitch-standards
deal with life and death,
reward and punishment,
giving and taking,
without these there is no Dào,
they quell disorder and prohibit violence,
promote the virtuous and good,
dismiss the unworthy,
correct the crooked to make them straight,
remove dangers to achieve peace,
straighten the bent to make them upright,
clarify the ways of giving and withholding,
opening and blocking,
riding the time and leveraging the situation,
to serve and command the people's hearts.
If an Emperor models on Yīn and Yáng, he will be encroached upon;
if a King follows the four seasons, he will be diminished;
if a Hegemon uses the six pitch-standards, he will be disgraced;
if a Ruler loses the standard and line, he will be deposed;
thus, the small practicing the great will be blocked and estranged,
the great practicing the small will be narrow and intolerant.
Lǎo zǐ said:
Vast land and numerous people
are not enough to constitute strength;
strong armor and sharp weapons
cannot be relied upon for victory;
high walls and deep moats
are not enough for security;
severe punishments and harsh laws
are not enough to establish authority.
Those who govern for preservation,
though small, will surely survive;
those who govern for ruin,
though large, will surely perish.
Thus, those skilled in defense
have none to resist them;
those skilled in battle
have none to fight them;
they ride the time and situation,
follow the people's desires,
and take the world.
Therefore, those skilled in governance
accumulate their Dé;
those skilled in using troops
store up their anger;
Dé accumulated makes the people usable;
anger stored establishes authority.
Thus, where culture penetrates deeply,
there authority subdues greatly;
where Dé is broadly applied,
there authority controls widely;
widely then I am strong and the enemy weak.
Those skilled in using troops
first weaken the enemy and then fight,
thus expending less than half effort for tenfold results.
A state of a thousand chariots
practicing cultural Dé will become kingly;
a state of ten thousand chariots
fond of using troops will perish;
the kingly army first ensures victory and then fights,
the defeated army first fights and then seeks victory,
this is not understanding the Dào.
Lǎo zǐ said:
The way of the noble person
uses stillness to cultivate the self,
frugality to nourish life.
Stillness then subordinates are not disturbed;
frugality then the people do not resent;
subordinates disturbed then governance is chaotic;
people resentful then Dé is thin;
governance chaotic, the worthy do not offer counsel;
Dé thin, the brave do not fight.
The chaotic ruler is not so;
possessing the wealth of the world in a day,
holding the power of a single ruler,
he exhausts the people's strength
to feed his desires of sight and sound,
his mind fixated on palaces, towers, and pavilions,
moats, parks, and enclosures,
fierce beasts and rare treasures;
while the poor starve,
tigers and wolves are satiated with fodder and livestock,
the people suffer cold and freezing,
the palaces are dressed in embroidered silks;
thus, the ruler hoards these useless things,
and the world cannot secure its nature and destiny.
Lǎo zǐ said:
Without indifference, one cannot illuminate Dé;
without tranquility, one cannot reach far;
without broad-mindedness, one cannot make decisive judgments;
using the eyes of the world to see,
the ears of the world to hear,
the wisdom of the world to ponder,
the strength of the world to strive,
thus commands can reach below,
and the sentiments of ministers can be heard above,
officials are cultivated and communicate,
ministers gather like spokes.
Not using rewards when pleased,
not using punishments when angry,
laws and decrees are clear but not harsh,
ears and eyes are informed but not darkened,
the realities of good and bad
are daily presented without opposition,
thus the worthy exhaust their wisdom,
the unworthy exert their strength,
those nearby are content with their nature,
those afar are drawn by his Dé,
this is the way to employ people.
Those who ride carriages and horses
travel a thousand miles without toil;
those who ride boats
cross rivers and seas without swimming.
If words are correct,
even from merchants or grass-cutters,
they should not be discarded;
if words are incorrect,
even from rulers or ministers,
they should not be used;
in matters of right and wrong,
one cannot judge by nobility or baseness.
If a plan is usable,
do not disdain the planner's status;
if words are practicable,
do not value eloquence;
the benighted ruler is not so;
ministers who offer sincerity and loyalty
are rarely not used up,
while he associates with the crooked and perverse,
the worthy cannot be seen,
the distant and lowly,
those exerting strength and loyalty cannot be heard.
Those who speak up
are refuted with words;
those who remonstrate
are punished with crimes;
wishing to pacify the world
and preserve all regions thus,
he is far from intelligence indeed.
Lǎozi said:
Those who can honor life,
though wealthy and noble, do not harm their bodies with excessive comforts,
though poor and lowly, do not burden their forms with pursuit of gain.
Now, inheriting the titles left by ancestors,
one must fear losing them gravely,
for life has been sustained for a long time,
yet to lose it lightly—
is that not delusion?
Hence,
"If one values governing the world as one values one's own body,
then the world can be entrusted to them;
if one loves governing the world as one loves one's own body,
then the world can be relied upon."
Wénzǐ asked about the foundation of governing a state.
Lǎozi said:
The foundation lies in governing oneself,
for it has never been heard that one who governs oneself well leads a state into chaos,
nor that one who is disordered in self leads a state to order.
Thus it is said:
"Cultivate it in oneself,
and one's virtue becomes genuine."
The reason the Dào is supremely subtle is that
a father cannot teach it to his son,
nor can a son receive it from his father.
Hence,
"The Dào that can be spoken of
is not the eternal Dào;
the name that can be named
is not the eternal name."
Wénzǐ asked:
How should one act so that the people feel close to their rulers?
Lǎozi said:
Employ them in due season and treat them with reverence and caution,
as if standing at the edge of a deep abyss,
as if treading on thin ice.
Between heaven and earth,
the good are those I nurture,
the not good are those I regard as enemies.
In the past, the ministers of the Xià and Shāng dynasties
turned against Jié and Zhòu as enemies,
and became subjects to Tāng and Wǔ.
The people of Sùshā
attacked their own ruler
and submitted to Shénnóngshì.
Therefore it is said:
"What others fear,
one cannot but fear."
Lǎozi said:
In governing great matters,
the Dào cannot be small;
with vast territory,
the system cannot be narrow;
in high position,
affairs cannot be complicated;
with a large population,
teaching cannot be harsh.
Complicated affairs are hard to manage,
harsh laws are hard to implement,
excessive demands are hard to satisfy.
Measuring inch by inch,
errors will arise by the yard;
weighing grain by grain,
mistakes will occur by the ton.
Weighing by the ton and measuring by the yard,
directness leads to few errors.
Broad comparisons are easy for wisdom,
intricate arguments are hard for insight.
Thus, what does not benefit order
but benefits chaos,
the sage does not do;
what is not useful
but increases waste,
the wise do not undertake.
Hence, achievements are never too concise,
affairs never too simplified,
demands never too modest.
Concise achievements are easily accomplished,
simplified affairs are easily managed,
modest demands are easily met,
and entrusting tasks to the multitude makes things easier.
Thus, petty arguments harm righteousness,
petty righteousness undermines the Dào.
A narrow Dào must be obstructed;
what is unobstructed must be simple.
The river winds and thus can flow far;
the mountain slopes gradually and thus can rise high;
the Dào moves freely and thus can transform.
Mastering one skill,
understanding one matter,
observing one ability
allows for detailed explanation
but not broad application.
In tuning music,
the small strings are tight,
the large strings are loose;
in establishing affairs,
the lowly toil,
the noble rest.
The words of the Dào say:
Vast and obscure,
it follows heaven's majesty,
united with the primordial in one breath.
Those who share this breath become emperors;
those who share its righteousness become kings;
those who share its achievements become hegemons;
those with none of these perish.
Thus, without speaking, there is trust;
without giving, there is benevolence;
without anger, there is authority—
this is how the heart of heaven moves and transforms.
Giving and being benevolent,
speaking and being trustworthy,
angry and authoritative—
this is done through essence and sincerity;
giving without benevolence,
speaking without trust,
angry without authority—
this is done through outward appearance.
Therefore, with the Dào to govern,
even if laws are few,
they suffice for order;
without the Dào to govern,
even if laws are numerous,
they suffice for chaos.
Lǎozi said:
When a whale is out of water,
it is controlled by ants;
when a ruler abandons his responsibilities
and competes with his ministers over affairs,
he becomes controlled by his officials.
By personally clinging to power,
those in positions adhere through obedience to gain favor,
while ministers conceal their wisdom and refrain from using it,
instead allowing matters to concentrate upon the ruler.
A ruler
who does not employ the capable but prefers to act personally
finds his wisdom increasingly strained and bears the burden alone.
When his strategies are exhausted below,
he cannot uphold justice;
when his actions falter in his position,
he cannot maintain control.
His wisdom is insufficient to govern,
his authority inadequate for punishment,
and thus he has no means to interact with the world.
If joy and anger are visible in his heart,
and desires are apparent outwardly,
then those in office deviate from righteousness to flatter their superior,
and officials
pervert the law to follow the trend.
Rewards do not match achievements,
punishments do not fit crimes,
leading to discord between high and low,
and resentment between ruler and ministers.
The百官 become troubled and confused, yet wisdom cannot resolve it;
false praises sprout, yet clarity cannot illuminate them.
Not recognizing his own faults, he instead blames himself,
causing the ruler to toil more
and the ministers to become more idle.
"This is like chopping wood in place of a master carpenter;
he who chops in place of a master carpenter
rarely avoids injuring his hand."
Racing against a horse on foot,
one's tendons may snap but still not catch up;
boarding a chariot and taking the reins,
the horse is steadied beneath the yoke.
With Bólè judging it,
and Wáng Liáng driving it,
an enlightened ruler rides it,
achieving a thousand lǐ without the toil of driving or judging—
this is skill in utilizing others' resources.
The way of a ruler
is non-action yet accomplishment,
having establishment but no personal preferences;
for action invites criticism,
and preferences invite flattery.
Criticism can lead to loss,
flattery can lead to seduction.
One who establishes yet is controlled by others
cannot govern the state effectively.
Therefore,
"he who is skilled at building cannot be uprooted,"
meaning that building is formless.
Only through spiritual transformation
can nothing overcome it.
When inner desires do not emerge, it is called being barred;
when external evils do not enter, it is called being closed.
Barred within and closed without,
what affair is not regulated?
Closed without and barred within,
what task is not accomplished?
Thus, without using it,
without acting on it,
yet it is useful,
and it is effective.
Without boastful words,
without coercive actions,
follow names to demand reality,
let officials manage their own duties.
Taking ignorance as the way,
and prohibiting harshness as the priority,
in this way, the affairs of the百官
each have their proper examination.
Lǎozi said:
Food is the foundation of the people,
the people are the basis of the state.
Therefore, the ruler
above follows the timing of heaven,
below exhausts the benefits of the earth,
and in the middle utilizes human strength.
Thus, all living things thrive and grow,
myriad beings multiply and flourish.
In spring, cut the withered;
in summer, gather various fruits;
in autumn, store vegetables and grains;
in winter, collect firewood and fuel,
to provide resources for the people,
so that in life there is no lack,
and in death, no unburied corpses.
The laws of the ancient kings
did not decimate herds to capture young animals,
did not drain ponds to fish,
did not burn forests to hunt.
Before the豺sacrificed prey,
nets could not be set in the wild;
before the獺sacrificed fish,
nets could not enter the waters;
before falcons struck,
snares could not be spread in the valleys;
before plants and trees shed leaves,
axes could not enter the mountains and forests;
before insects hibernated,
fire could not be used in fields.
Pregnant animals were not killed,
eggs and nestlings were not taken.
Fish shorter than a chǐ were not caught,
dogs and pigs not a year old were not eaten.
Thus, the growth of all things is like steam rising.
The ancient kings responded to the seasons and prepared accordingly—
this is the way to enrich the state and benefit the people.
It is not about seeing with eyes or walking with feet;
if the desire to benefit the people is never forgotten in heart,
then the people will naturally be prepared.
Lǎozi said:
In ancient times,
enlightened rulers took from below with moderation,
and supported themselves with restraint.
They necessarily calculated the year's harvest,
measured the people's stores,
knew the numbers of surplus and shortage,
and only then took their dues.
In this way,
they could receive what heaven and earth provided
and avoid the plight of hunger and cold.
Compassionate towards the people,
if the state had hungry individuals,
they did not eat multiple flavors;
if the people suffered from cold,
they did not wear furs in winter.
Sharing hardships and joys with the people,
then under heaven, there were no sorrowful people.
Foolish rulers, however, are not so;
they take from the people without considering their strength,
demand from below without measuring their stores.
Men and women cannot pursue farming and weaving
to meet the ruler's demands;
strength is exhausted, resources spent,
with morning but no evening,
ruler and ministers resent each other.
Moreover, in making a living,
one person treading the plow to farm
cannot exceed ten mǔ,
the harvest from average land not surpassing four dàn,
with wife, children, and the elderly relying on it for food.
If sometimes disaster strikes,
and they cannot meet the ruler's demands,
then human life becomes pitiable.
Greedy rulers and tyrants
drain their people like drying up fish,
to satisfy limitless desires,
so that the common people do not receive heaven's harmony
or tread earth's virtue.
Lǎozi said:
Of heaven and earth's energies,
none is greater than harmony.
Harmony means
yīn and yáng are balanced,
day and night divided,
thus all things are born at the spring equinox
and mature at the autumn equinox.
Both birth and maturity
must obtain the essence of harmony.
Therefore, accumulated yīn does not produce,
accumulated yáng does not transform;
only when yīn and yáng interact
can harmony be achieved.
Thus, the way of the sage
is broad yet stern,
strict yet gentle,
soft yet straight,
fierce yet benevolent.
For too rigid leads to breakage,
too soft leads to curling;
the right path lies between rigidity and softness.
The line as a measure
can be rolled and carried,
pulled and extended;
it can be straightened and dried,
long without being horizontal,
short without being exhausted,
straight without being rigid—
thus the sage embodies it.
For kindness pushed leads to weakness,
weakness leads to lack of authority;
strictness pushed leads to harshness,
harshness leads to disharmony;
love pushed leads to indulgence,
indulgence leads to lack of order;
punishment pushed leads to calamity,
calamity leads to lack of intimacy.
Therefore, harmony is valued.
Lǎozi said:
The reason a state survives
is because it attains the Dào,
the reason it perishes
is because the principles are obstructed.
Thus, the sage observes transformations to discern their signs.
Virtue has its flourishing and decline,
and the winds are the first sprouts.
Therefore, those who attain and preserve the Dào,
though small, will surely become great;
those who have signs of perishing,
though established, will surely fail.
The perishing of a state
cannot rely on its size,
the practice of the Dào
cannot be slighted even in small matters.
Thus, survival lies in attaining the Dào,
not in being small;
perishing lies in losing the Dào,
not in being large.
Therefore, the rulers of chaotic states
strive for territorial expansion,
but do not strive for rén and yì;
they seek high positions,
but do not seek the Dào and virtue.
This is to abandon what ensures survival
and create what leads to destruction.
If above, they disrupt the brightness of the three luminaries,
and below, they lose the hearts of the myriad people,
who would not be able to seize power?
Thus, examine what lies within oneself,
and do not blame others.
In ancient times, those who were rulers,
practicing deeply were called the Dào and virtue,
practicing shallowly were called rén and yì,
practicing minimally were called propriety and wisdom.
These six
are the guiding principles of the state.
Practicing them deeply brings abundant blessings,
practicing them shallowly brings meager blessings,
practicing them fully makes one prevail over the world.
In ancient times, cultivating the Dào and virtue rectified the world,
cultivating rén and yì rectified a state,
cultivating propriety and wisdom rectified a village.
Those with abundant virtue achieve greatness,
those with meager virtue achieve smallness.
Thus, the Dào is not established by might and force,
not won by strength and hardness,
not gained by greed and contention.
It is established by the world extending itself,
won by the world submitting of its own accord,
gained by the world giving it,
not by taking it for oneself.
Thus, the feminine is established,
the soft and weak prevail,
rén and yì are gained,
by not contending, none can contend with you.
Therefore, the Dào in the world
is like rivers and seas.
The way of Heaven
is that those who act ruin it,
those who grasp lose it.
Those who desire great fame and seek it through contention,
I see that they do not attain it;
even if they grasp and gain it,
it does not remain.
Fame cannot be sought and obtained;
it lies in the world giving it.
Those who give it submit to it;
what the world submits to
is virtue.
Thus it is said:
Those with superior virtue are submitted to by the world,
those with superior rén are submitted to within the seas,
those with superior yì are submitted to by a state,
those with superior propriety are submitted to by a village.
Without these four,
the people do not submit.
Without submission, arms are used;
using arms is the way of danger.
Therefore it is said:
"Arms
are instruments of ill omen,
to be used only when unavoidable."
Using them kills and wounds people;
do not glorify victory.
Thus it is said:
"In the place of death,
thorns and brambles grow;
mourn it with sorrow,
dwell on it with funeral rites."
Therefore, the noble person strives for the Dào and virtue
and does not rely on heavy arms.
Wénzǐ asked:
"Why are benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom considered inferior to the Way and its virtue?"
Lǎozǐ said:
"Those who practice benevolence
must base it on sorrow and joy,
those who practice righteousness
must demonstrate it through giving and taking.
Throughout the world,
sorrow and joy cannot be universally applied,
and even exhausting the treasury's wealth
is insufficient to provide for all people.
Therefore, we know it is better to cultivate the Way and practice virtue,
following the nature of heaven and earth,
so all things correct themselves and the world is provided for,
with benevolence and righteousness naturally adhering.
'Thus the great man dwells in the thick,
not in the thin.'
Now propriety
is the ornament of substance,
and benevolence
is the manifestation of kindness.
Therefore propriety is established according to human feelings,
not exceeding their substance,
and benevolence does not overflow with kindness.
Grief is embraced in genuine feeling,
and burying the dead is called benevolence.
Nourishing life does not force people beyond their capabilities,
nor does it prevent them from what they cannot stop.
When measures do not lose their appropriateness,
blame and praise have no cause to arise.
Thus making music should suffice to unite joy,
not going beyond harmony,
clarifying the distinction between life and death,
and understanding the appropriateness of extravagance and frugality.
The decadent age, however, is not like this:
words and actions contradict each other,
inner feelings and outer appearance are opposed,
propriety is adorned with complexity,
music is disturbed with excess,
customs are corrupted in the world,
and blame and praise gather at court.
Therefore the perfect person abandons and does not use these.
If a man races with a fine horse,
the man cannot surpass the horse,
but if he rides in a carriage,
the horse cannot surpass the man.
Thus those skilled in using the Way
ride on others' resources to achieve merit,
using what they can do
to support what they cannot.
When the ruler provides them with timely opportunities,
the people repay him with wealth;
when the ruler treats them with propriety,
the people repay him with their lives.
Thus there are endangered states but no secure rulers,
and anxious rulers but no happy ministers.
Virtue exceeding one's position brings honor,
while emolument exceeding one's virtue brings misfortune.
Virtue's honor asks for no high rank,
righteous acquisition takes not much.
Those not honored for virtue
usurp positions;
those acquiring not by righteousness
steal wealth.
The sage is content with poverty and delights in the Way,
not harming life with desires,
not burdening himself with profit.
Therefore he does not violate righteousness to take recklessly.
In ancient times, none without virtue were honored,
none without ability were appointed,
none without merit were rewarded,
none without crime were punished.
They advanced people according to propriety,
and dismissed people according to righteousness.
In the age of petty men,
advancing people is like lifting them to heaven,
dismissing people is like pushing them into abyss.
Speaking of antiquity is to criticize the present.
Judging horses, we err regarding the lean;
selecting scholars, we err regarding the poor.
Fat pigs fill the kitchen,
but bony ones don't serve in office.
The superior man examines the substance,
not trusting slanderous words.
The ruler errs yet not remonstrated -
this is not loyal ministers;
remonstrating yet not heeded -
this is the ruler's lack of clarity.
The people drown yet not concerned -
this is not a worthy ruler.
Thus maintaining integrity and dying for crises
is the duty of ministers,
while clothing the cold and feeding the hungry
is the kindness of a compassionate father.
The great serving the small is called perverting people,
the small offending the great is called defying heaven.
Though one may ascend to heaven before,
one must sink into abyss after.
Thus in villages, age determines precedence,
the old and poor are not abandoned;
at court, rank determines order,
the honored and humble have differences.
Honoring the noble
means they are close to the ruler;
respecting the elderly
means they are close to parents;
revering elders
means they are close to elder brothers.
Those born noble become arrogant,
those born rich become extravagant.
Thus if the rich and noble don't use the bright Way for self-reflection,
few can avoid wrongdoing.
Studying without weariness
is how to cultivate oneself;
teaching without fatigue
is how to govern the people.
With worthy teachers and good friends,
few would abandon them for wrongdoing.
Knowing the worthy is called wisdom,
loving the worthy is called benevolence,
honoring the worthy is called righteousness,
respecting the worthy is called propriety,
delighting in the worthy is called music.
Those in ancient times skilled at governing the world
did nothing yet nothing was left undone.
Thus governing the world requires proper demeanor,
and attaining this demeanor,
one does nothing yet achieves merit.
Not attaining this demeanor,
every action brings misfortune.
The proper demeanor for governing the world is:
'Cautious, as if crossing winter streams;
hesitant, as if fearing neighbors;
dignified, as being a guest;
melting, like ice turning to liquid;
genuine, like unworked wood;
merged, like turbid water;
vast, like valleys'
—this is called the world's proper demeanor.
'Cautious, as if crossing winter streams'
means not daring to act;
'hesitant, as if fearing neighbors'
means fearing self-harm;
'dignified, as being a guest'
means carefully maintaining respect;
'melting, like ice turning to liquid'
means not daring to accumulate and store;
'genuine, like unworked wood'
means not daring to be sharp and finished;
'merged, like turbid water'
means not daring to be clear and bright;
'vast, like valleys'
means not daring to be full and overflowing.
Advancing but not daring to act
means retreating and not daring to take the lead;
fearing self-harm
means preserving weakness and not daring to be proud;
carefully maintaining respect
means humbling oneself to honor others;
not daring to accumulate and store
means impairing oneself and not daring to be firm;
not daring to be sharp and finished
means accepting incompleteness and not daring to be whole;
not daring to be clear and bright
means dwelling in turbidity and disgrace and not daring to be fresh;
not daring to be full and overflowing
means seeing insufficiency and not daring to consider oneself worthy.
Now the Way
retreats, thus it can lead;
preserves weakness, thus it can be proud;
